items.title: dotdash
items.text:
dotdash gets devices in a restricted network out to the open internet through a server of yours outside it. It comes as five morzer bundles, released together from one tag:

Bundle Runs on What it does dotdash a server outside the restricted network Xray REALITY on 443 in front of a cover site; everything leaves through your upstream proxy dotdash-relay a machine inside the restricted network carries phones, clients and canaries on to the server while only some addresses get through dotdash-client a Linux machine on the client side a proxy port, the whole machine, or a whole LAN through dotdash dotdash-canary a machine inside the restricted network connects as a device would, and alerts when it can't get through dotdash-acme-dns a small machine of its own answers the DNS-01 checks of the servers' and relays' wildcard certificates

Start with the server: its tasks print the relay's, the client's and the canary's setup. The client and the canary reach it as phones do, directly or through a relay.

items.title: What every machine needs
items.text:
Docker ≥ 28 with Compose ≥ 2.35, sops, age, and morzer ≥ 0.18.0. On a fresh Debian or Ubuntu machine, bootstrap.sh installs them, turns on security updates, and sets SSH to keys only:

curl -fsSLO https://morzecrew.github.io/dotdash/bootstrap.sh
less bootstrap.sh && sudo bash bootstrap.sh

Installing morzer by hand: install.sh --dir /usr/local/bin. sudo and morzer's timers don't look in ~/.local/bin.

Every bundle ships the key it is signed with: morzer init prints it, trusts it, and requires every later release to be signed by it.

items.title: Releases
items.text:
Tag ghcr.io/morzecrew/<bundle>:stable the newest release (vX.Y.Z tags), release key ghcr.io/morzecrew/<bundle>:X.Y.Z one release ghcr.io/morzecrew/<bundle>:main every push to main, dev key; may be broken

<bundle> is dotdash-server, dotdash-relay, dotdash-client, dotdash-canary or dotdash-acme-dns. These docs are versioned with the releases: the version menu shows each released minor, and dev follows main.

items.title: Manager
items.text:
dotdash-manager runs a whole network from one roster: servers, relays, canaries, client machines and devices. It makes the keys the servers share, gives every server and relay the same devices, writes the servers' relays and the relays' way to the servers from what each machine reports, and keeps canaries and clients pointed at them.

It never logs in to a machine. Each machine follows it through morzer's desired state: it pulls a signed, encrypted document from a bucket every 15 minutes and publishes its facts there. The manager runs where you keep the authority key, never on a managed machine.

network.toml ──▶ dotdash-manager sync ──▶ one document per machine ──▶ the bucket ──▶ each machine
                         ▲                                                  │
                         └──────────── servers' and relays' facts ◀─────────┘

It needs morzer and age-keygen beside it, and installs with uv at the tag of the release your machines run, such as v0.7.0:

uv tool install "git+https://github.com/morzecrew/dotdash@<tag>#subdirectory=manager"

To move to a later release, run it again with that tag and --force.

items.title: Set it up
items.text:
morzer state key generate ./authority.key   # prints the public key: authority below
age-keygen -o ./authority.age               # facts are encrypted to it

Keep both off the machines. Whoever holds authority.key sets everything the bundles let it, devices and keys included.

Then the roster, network.toml:

target = "s3://dotdash-state/net"           # a bucket every machine reaches
credentials = "./target-credential.yaml"    # morzer's credential document for it
key = "./authority.key"
identity = "./authority.age"
authority = "RWQ…"                          # what state key generate printed
subscription = true                         # every device gets a subscription URL
ipv6 = "allow"                              # or block, on the relays
direct = false                              # optional: devices reach servers only through relays and CDNs
devices = ["phone", "laptop"]

[pools]                                     # optional: the server's pools, member by member
a = ["laptop", "203.0.113.5"]

[[server]]
name = "a"
cdn_hosts = ["cdn.example.net"]             # optional: this server's cdn_hosts

[[relay]]
name = "r1"
provider = "hoster-a"                       # optional: your own name for who hosts it
address_since = 2026-11-01                  # optional: since when it has this address
standby = true                              # optional: devices use it only once every other link fails
via = ["r0"]                                # optional: relays it goes through instead of the servers
via_link = "xhttp"                          # optional, with via: reality (the default) or xhttp through their own sites

[[canary]]
name = "c1"
watches = "r1"                              # a server or a relay

[[client]]
name = "home"
device = "phone"                            # the device whose subscription it follows

With direct = false the servers keep their addresses out of devices' links (direct), and client machines fetch their subscription through an own-site relay, waiting for one. Left out, each server keeps its own setting.

A relay with via goes through those relays instead of the servers (Through another relay): they let it in by its own id, and its document waits for their facts. A relay running a release from before via waits to be updated rather than going to the servers.

Names are lowercase letters, digits and dashes. relay- and canary- start the names the manager gives relays' and canaries' own devices. A field the roster doesn't know is refused, so a mistyped one can't pass unnoticed.

items.title: Add a machine
items.text:
Name it in the roster first, run sync so the servers learn its device, then pipe join's script to the new machine over ssh, and what it prints back to joined:

dotdash-manager sync
dotdash-manager join r1 --site site.example.net --entry-host 203.0.113.7 \
  | ssh root@203.0.113.7 sh | dotdash-manager joined r1
dotdash-manager sync          # r1 gets its document

The script installs what the machine lacks (scripts/bootstrap.sh, as on a fresh Debian or Ubuntu), runs its init with the values it needs, sets its secrets, points it at the manager and applies. On a machine where the bundle is installed already, it leaves the installation as it is and only points it at the manager, whose document brings the rest. Its last line carries the machine's installation id and signing key, which joined keeps in the manager's state, so the next sync sends the machine its document. The rest of its output passes through, so a failure shows; joined then keeps nothing, and the script can run again.

What each kind needs to be installed:

  • A server: --domain and --upstreams <file>, its ways out, one per line. It comes up on keys of its own: the first document replaces them, and relays, canaries and clients move to it once its facts show the manager's key. A relay, canary or client waits for a server that has.
  • A relay: --site and --entry-host (a neighbour's site, and the address devices reach it at), or --domain for one of its own site.
  • A canary or a client: nothing more.

Backups are encrypted to the identity's age recipient, or to --recovery. The script holds the machine's credentials: send it to that machine only. A roster entry's own id and key, as earlier releases had you write them, still win over what joined kept.

items.title: Moving a running network
items.text:
A network set up by hand moves to the manager without devices noticing: the manager takes a running server's keys and its devices' ids instead of making its own, so devices keep their links and subscription URLs. Name the server, its relays and the devices in the roster under the names the server already uses (client-config prints them), then, before the first sync:

dotdash-manager adopt a       # prints what to run on server a
ssh root@a.example 'sudo sh -c …' | dotdash-manager adopt a

It says which devices keep their links, which are new to the server, and which the server has but the roster doesn't, which lose access at the next sync unless you add them. Finish a key rotation first: only the current key is taken. Once the manager has published, adopt refuses, since it would change the keys on every machine again; --force when that is meant.

Then join every machine as above, the running server and relays included, with no options: the script finds them installed and only points them at the manager. Relays keep their own keys, so devices keep their relay links too.

items.title: Keep it current
items.text:
dotdash-manager sync --dry-run   # what would change
dotdash-manager sync
dotdash-manager status           # what each machine applied and refused

sync publishes only documents that changed, and renews the rest every three days: a document expires after seven. Run it from a timer to keep it ahead of that. A device added to devices reaches every server and relay at the next sync; one removed loses its access everywhere, each machine within its next cycle.

The manager keeps what it made in dotdash-state.json beside the roster: the shared keys, every device's id and the client machines' proxy passwords. It is written with mode 0600 and holds every credential in the network: back it up like authority.key. One run at a time changes it: a run holds dotdash-state.lock beside it, and another started meanwhile, such as a timer's sync during a rotate, waits for it. sync --dry-run leaves it as it was.

items.title: Burnt relays
items.text:
Before every fleet publish, about hourly, each canary that follows the manager reports whether each of its paths to the server or relay it watches gets through. When every canary watching a relay got through none of its paths three readings in a row, sync leaves that relay out of the servers' relays and pools, and of client machines' subscription URLs, and says so. A reading counts only beside the newest of the other canaries watching the same relay within 90 minutes, so a canary gone quiet can't hold the relay up with an old success:

burnt: relay r1: its canaries got through none of its paths in 3 readings; left out of the servers' relays and pools until a canary gets through again; its own fleet row (40m old) says it runs: blocked on the way, not down; replace it

Devices stop getting its links at their next subscription refresh. The relay keeps its own document and its canaries keep watching it, so a single reading that gets through brings it back. To replace it, add a relay on a fresh address, then take the burnt one out of the roster.

The verdict also says what the relay's own fleet row, which it publishes hourly, says of it. A relay whose row is fresh and whose services all run is blocked on the way, and replacing its address is the fix. One whose row has gone quiet for three hours, or whose services aren't all running, is likelier down than blocked: the verdict says to fix it first, and doesn't say to replace it. A row that doesn't verify says nothing either way.

  • A canary whose own network is down says nothing, given a control_url: a site its network reaches without dotdash. A reading where that fails doesn't count. Without one, an offline canary looks like a burnt relay.
  • Every relay at once is kept. If every relay would be left out in the same sync, the manager keeps them all and says to check the canaries' network instead.
  • A burnt server is only reported. Relays reach the servers, so leaving one out would cut them off.
  • A relay no canary watches is never judged. Run canaries where devices are: on a mobile line.
  • Neither is a CDN-only relay. Its canaries check its own address, which no device gets.

items.title: Spare relays
items.text:
A burnt relay waits for you to replace it. A spare takes its place at the next sync instead, about an hour after the third failed reading. Install a relay as usual, add it to the roster with spare = true, and point a canary at it:

[[relay]]
name = "r3"
spare = true

[[canary]]
name = "c3"
watches = "r3"

A spare gets its document and runs like any relay, and its canary watches it, but devices don't get it: it's out of the servers' relays and pools. When a relay burns, the first spare that isn't burnt itself stands in for it, and takes its place in the pools. Spares a canary has got through to go first, in roster order; one no canary has checked yet still stands in, and sync says to check it:

spare: r3 stands in for burnt relay r1, in its pools; replace r1, then make r3 a regular relay (spare = false) and add a new spare

A spare stands in only while the relay it replaces is burnt. If a canary gets through to that relay again, it's back and the spare waits again. Each burnt relay takes one spare, in roster order; with none left, sync says so.

A spare burnt while it waits was blocked without any device holding its address: for its network's range, say, or found by scanning. That's worth knowing when you pick where the next one goes.

items.title: How long relays last
items.text:
Every sync logs what changed: a server or relay its canaries start watching, one that burns or comes back, one that leaves the roster, a path going off or on, a spare standing in or waiting again. report reads that log:

dotdash-manager report

machine      kind    status   watched          lasted burns     down  paths off
s            server  up       2026-11-01      14d 3h+     0        -  -
r1           relay   burnt    2026-11-01       10d 0h     2    4d 2h  reality×1
r2           relay   up       2026-11-03      12d 1h+     0        -  -
r3           spare   standing 2026-11-05            -     0        -  -; stood in 1×
old          gone    gone     2026-10-20        4d 0h     1    1d 0h  -

relays: 2 burnt, lasting 7d 0h at the median
        1 never burnt, watched 12d 1h so far
        1 burn(s) in the last 30 days; spares waiting: none

lasted runs from the first reading to the first burn, or until now with a + for one that hasn't burnt yet; down adds up the time it spent burnt. A relay taken out of the roster stays in the report, as gone: how long the ones you replaced lasted is what tells whether a change (a transport, a network, a provider) makes the next ones last longer. The log keeps the newest 2000 events, and starts with the first sync of a manager that has it.

Then how long each path lasted before it was first blocked, a burn included, and the median per path: which transport lasts.

paths: how long each lasted before it was first blocked (+: never yet)
machine             reality          xhttp  xhttp-reality           mkcp      hysteria2
r1                   10d 0h          4d 2h              -              -        16d 0h+
r2                  16d 0h+        16d 0h+              -              -        16d 0h+
old                   4d 0h              -              -              -              -
median to first block: reality 7d 0h (2 blocked, 1 never); xhttp 4d 2h (1 blocked, 1 never); hysteria2 never blocked (2, 16d 0h longest)

With provider, and address_since if you know it, on servers and relays in the roster, the lifetimes also add up per provider, and with how old the addresses were when their canaries first watched them. Both are your own record: nothing is looked up, and sync keeps them for machines you take out of the roster.

by provider (the roster's provider), servers and relays: burnt and their median life, never burnt
hoster-a         2 burnt, 7d 0h at the median; addresses 3d 0h old when first watched, at the median
hoster-b         0 burnt; 1 never burnt (16d 0h so far)

items.title: Where the time goes
items.text:
Each canary's facts time its paths and its own network (latency_ms and direct_ms), and sync keeps each machine's last 24 readings. The report ends with their medians:

latency, ms (median of the last readings): the canaries' own network, then each path through it
s            network    90   reality 210, xhttp 180
r1           network   100   reality 290 (+80 over the servers)

A path's time less network is what dotdash adds: the target, its upstream and the site. For a relay, the figure in brackets is what it adds over the servers on the same path, which is the hop to the server. That's close enough to compare relays, but canaries sit on different networks, so it is no exact measure. A machine whose canaries predate these timings is left out until they update.

items.title: Rotating the REALITY key
items.text:
rotate changes the servers' REALITY key with no device cut off, over their second key (Rotating the REALITY key), in three steps, each published by the next sync:

dotdash-manager rotate start     # the next key second on the servers; their canaries move to it
dotdash-manager sync
dotdash-manager rotate swap      # once a canary got through on it: the key now, the old one second
dotdash-manager sync
dotdash-manager rotate finish    # a week later: the old key off
dotdash-manager sync
  • start gives the servers a next key as their second. Only the canaries watching servers move to it: devices and relays keep the current key.
  • swap refuses until one of those canaries has got REALITY through on the next key since start. It then makes the next key the servers' key and keeps the old one second. Subscriptions, client machines and relays move to the new key, and devices still on the old one keep getting in.
  • finish refuses for a week after swap, the devices' time to fetch their subscriptions or get new links. It then turns the old key off.
  • rotate alone says where it stands. --force skips the canary check or the week, when you know better.

items.title: Blocked paths
items.text:
Short of burnt, a relay can lose one path while its others get through: its REALITY port cut while XHTTP through its own site still answers, mKCP dropped, or one path's connections frozen after their first few kilobytes, which a canary's freeze download catches. When every canary watching a relay got through none of its readings on one path three times in a row, and another path got through, sync puts that path on the relay's line as off=:

blocked: relay r1: reality got through for none of its canaries in 3 readings; devices get its other paths until one gets through again

Devices then get only its other links through it (and its CDN links, which canaries don't check), at their next subscription refresh. A reading where the path gets through again takes it off.

  • A path blocked on every relay that has it is kept. That's likelier the canaries' network refusing the transport than every relay losing it at once, so the manager says to check that network instead.
  • A server's blocked paths are only reported, as a burnt server is.
  • A server released before off= ignores the field and gives devices every link through the relay, as before.

items.title: A name blocked by SNI
items.text:
A box can block a server's name by the SNI in each ClientHello, reassembling TCP but reading one TLS record at a time. Its canaries see REALITY fail while REALITY with its hello split into small TLS records gets through. After three readings like that in a row, sync sets the server's hello_split:

split: server a: REALITY gets through only with its hello split into TLS records, a block on its name by SNI; devices' Xray configs split it (hello_split), share links can't
  • Who it reaches. Devices running Xray from their subscription's config, such as dotdash-client or an app on client-config --full, split their REALITY hello to that server from their next refresh. Share links can't carry it, so apps on links keep failing there and use another path.
  • Off again. It goes off once REALITY gets through again, or once the split fails too.
  • Why not always on. The split hello is a fingerprint of its own, which a classifier picks up (dotdash-lab #33).
  • Relays too. A relay's canaries can find the same of its site's name. Its line then gets split beside off=reality. Share links lose REALITY through it, as for any blocked path, while devices' Xray configs keep it, split. A burnt relay stays out.

items.title: What it leaves alone
items.text: The upstreams, ports, profiles, domains and anything else a machine alone knows stay the operator's, set on that machine as before. A value the manager sets is refused by config set on the machine while sync is on; --force changes it until the next document.

items.title: Keep more than one way in
items.text: Some networks let through only a set list of addresses, for a region or for mobile data, and your servers need not be on it. The server then stops answering devices there, while a relay inside that network and a local CDN may still answer. Set them up and hand everything out before restrictions start, while devices still reach the server.

items.title: Before
items.text:
1. A relay with a site of its own (set one up), in a network that stays reachable. Give relay-entry the relay's domain rather than its IP: links and subscription URLs then name the domain, and moving the relay to a new address only takes a DNS change.
  2. A canary on the kind of line devices use (canary), checking the relay. It alerts you when a way in stops working for devices like yours.
  3. A local CDN, as one more way in (CDN). Expect the account to be closed one day.
  4. Every device gets its links again once the relay and the CDN are in. With subscriptions on, give a device inside the restricted network its subscription URL through the relay (through the relay … in client-config), not the server's. Its app then keeps refreshing its links while restrictions last.
  5. Test on a phone on the network you care about, using mobile data with Wi-Fi off and the relay link alone.

items.title: During
items.text:
• An app that can't fetch its subscription keeps the links it already has. With the URL through the relay, it keeps refreshing: new relays, revocations and rotated keys still reach it.
  • The Xray config from client-config uses whichever of the server, the relays and the CDNs answers, on its own. An app holding several links lets the user pick one that works.
  • Pages stall after a few kilobytes while chat still works: the network freezes a connection to an address abroad once it has carried its first 16-20 KB, and leaves it open and silent. Every TCP link to the server fails this way, REALITY and XHTTP alike, and small checks still pass, so an app may keep picking a frozen link. What gets through is a link to an address inside the network, a relay's or a local CDN's, or Hysteria2 where UDP passes (dotdash-lab #64 froze TCP alone; what such a network does to UDP is untested). A canary on that network reports it as blocked_by: freeze, with the bytes it got under stalled.
  • To hand a link over, show its QR code in person, send a file, or use any channel that still gets through. A link or subscription URL is a credential that also names your relay, so avoid a messenger whose operator may read or hand over messages. If a link may have leaked, delete the device from vless_clients and give it a new one.
  • If a relay's address is blocked, move the relay to a new machine or address under the same domain. Its links and subscription URLs work again as soon as DNS points there. Devices with links through other relays carry on meanwhile.

items.title: Canary
items.text: The dotdash-canary bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-canary) runs on a machine inside the network you worry about. It connects to a dotdash server, or a relay, as a device would, and fails doctor when it can't get through: you hear about a block before your users do. It needs Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh), and no open port.

items.title: Install
items.text:
1. On the server, add a <uuid> canary line to vless_clients, then print the canary's setup:

    sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients
sudo morzer task run canary-config --output -- canary

  2. On the canary machine, run what that printed: init, four secrets, apply. The recovery recipient can be the server's own.

  3. Alerts: add a notify target and run doctor every 10 minutes:

    sudo morzer notify target add https://hooks.example/morzer
sudo morzer config set doctor.schedule='*:0/10'

items.title: What it checks
items.text:
By default the canary checks REALITY on 443. Profiles add a transport:

init flag Also checks --profile xhttp XHTTP, through the server's cover site --profile xhttp-reality XHTTP with REALITY, on its own port --profile mkcp mKCP, on its own UDP port --profile hysteria2 Hysteria2, on its own UDP port, logging in as the canary's id

Each check fetches probe_url through dotdash, in up to three tries.

To measure rather than check, measure runs each transport a number of times and prints the success rate, timeouts and latency as JSON, then downloads download_url three times through each and adds the median Mbit/s:

sudo morzer task run measure --output -- 50

A canary that follows the manager tells it, before every fleet publish, whether each transport gets through (facts), and the manager leaves a relay its canaries can't get through out of devices' links.

Getting through takes more than probe_url's fetch. A network's DPI may freeze a connection to a hosting address abroad after its first 16-20 KB, leaving it open and silent, and a fetch that small never reaches the mark. So facts then downloads freeze_url (64 KB) through each transport. A download that stops partway, with no byte for 8 seconds or cut, twice running, counts the transport as not getting through, and facts gives the bytes it got under stalled. A download that gets no byte at all says nothing about a freeze (freeze_url's own host may be down) and leaves the transport as probe_url found it.

The same goes the other way, for a network that counts what a device sends: facts uploads 64 KB to freeze_up_url through each transport. An upload that gets no answer for 8 seconds, twice running, counts the transport as not getting through, named under stalled_up; one that fails sooner (refused, an error page) says nothing about a freeze. Set control_url to a site this canary's network reaches without dotdash, so the canary's own outage isn't read as its target burnt:

sudo morzer config set control_url=https://www.example.net/

facts also times things, to 10 ms. latency_ms gives each transport that gets through the time its probe_url fetch took on a new connection: this network's leg, the target's, and on to the site. direct_ms is control_url's fetch without dotdash, this network's leg alone. The manager's report sets one against the other.

When REALITY fails, facts says what stops it, from the canary's own network, as blocked_by:

blocked_by What the canary found freeze connections freeze partway (the freeze checks above) ip no TCP connection to the server's port at all: a block on its address sni a connection, and REALITY gets through with its hello split: a block on the name by SNI tls a connection, but REALITY fails even split: a block on the TLS, or on REALITY itself

The manager names it in its verdicts. With ipv6_url set to an address reachable over IPv6 alone, facts also fetches it through each transport, as ipv6: whether the server carries devices' IPv6 that way.

facts also asks a DNS server (udp_target, 1.1.1.1:53) over UDP through each transport and gives the result as udp: whether the server carries devices' UDP (upstream_udp), which decides what WebRTC shows behind a TUN (WebRTC).

facts also tries REALITY with its ClientHello split into small TLS records, sent apart, and gives the result as reality_split. REALITY failing while the split one gets through is a box blocking the server's name by SNI, reassembling TCP but not TLS records, and the manager then hands devices the split.

items.title: Several servers, and relays
items.text: A canary watches one server. With several servers, canary-config prints how to point a canary at each of the others. To watch a relay instead, run the commands its relay-entry prints on the canary, without the xhttp profiles: the canary then connects through the relay, as a phone on that network would. A relay with Hysteria2 of its own prints the hysteria2 profile and its port too, and the canary checks it under the relay's own site's certificate. A canary that follows the manager gets that port from it.

items.title: On a mobile line
items.text: Mobile networks can be restricted where wired lines are not, so a canary on a wired line can't see what phones see. Run one on a small machine with a USB mobile modem on the network you care about, with mobile data as its only way out, and point it at a relay. One for each network and region that matters. A canary that fails there while the relay itself passes doctor means the relay's address no longer gets through for devices.

items.title: Reference
items.text: Parameter Default dotdash_server none, given at init the server's domain, sent as the TLS server name; a relay's site dotdash_address none, given at init where to connect: normally the same domain; an IP, a CDN's name, or a relay's address dotdash_port 443 the server's https_port dotdash_xhttp_reality_port 8443 the server's xhttp_reality_port dotdash_kcp_port 8447 the server's kcp_port dotdash_kcp_header dtls the server's kcp_header dotdash_kcp_open none the server's kcp_open dotdash_hysteria2_port 443 the server's hysteria2_port, or a relay's dotdash_hysteria2_pin none the SHA-256 of a certificate Hysteria2 trusts in place of the public CAs, as openssl x509 -fingerprint -sha256 prints it, for a server whose certificate no public CA signed; none checks it as devices do dotdash_public_key none, given at init the REALITY public key, the pbk of a link probe_url https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 what each check fetches through dotdash; any 2xx is healthy download_url https://speed.cloudflare.com/__down?bytes=1000000 what measure downloads for its Mbit/s, https:// only; none skips the downloads control_url none a site this canary's network reaches without dotdash, which facts fetches directly; none for no such check freeze_url https://speed.cloudflare.com/__down?bytes=65536 what facts downloads through each transport after probe_url, past the 16-20 KB a freeze lets through, https:// only; none skips it freeze_up_url https://speed.cloudflare.com/__up where facts uploads 64 KB through each transport, for a freeze counted on what the device sends, https:// only; none skips it Secret dotdash_id the canary's id, its line in the server's vless_clients dotdash_encryption the encryption= value of a link dotdash_short_id the sid= value of a REALITY link dotdash_kcp_seed the seed= value of an mKCP link, for --profile mkcp dotdash_xhttp_path the path= value of an XHTTP link, without the leading %2F Task measure --output -- [count] [url] [timeout] each transport count times (20 by default), as JSON facts --output what it watches, whether each transport gets through (freeze_url included), the bytes a stopped download got, and whether control_url answers, as JSON; what the manager reads

items.title: Client
items.text:
The dotdash-client bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-client) runs on a Linux machine on the client side: a home server, a Raspberry Pi, an office VM. It runs Xray from one device's subscription URL and sends traffic through dotdash, over whichever of that device's links answers fastest.

Three ways in, from least to most:

What goes through dotdash Set up Proxy port apps set to use a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy, on this machine or, shared, on the LAN the default Whole machine every connection on this machine, its containers' too, with no proxy settings the tun profile LAN gateway every device whose gateway is this machine tun with gateway=true

Rules send chosen destinations around dotdash or refuse them; everything else goes through it. With dotdash out of reach, nothing leaves around it.

items.title: Install
items.text:
The machine needs Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh).

  1. On the server, with subscriptions on, add a device for this machine, a <uuid> home line in vless_clients, and print its URL:

    sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- home

  2. On the client machine:

    morzer secret recipients generate-recovery-key ~/client-recovery.key   # keep it off the machine
sudo morzer init --release oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-client:stable \
  --recovery-recipient age1…
sudo morzer secret set subscription_url    # the URL from step 1
sudo morzer apply

  3. Check that the port gets out through dotdash; 204 means it does:

    curl --proxy socks5h://127.0.0.1:7890 https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 -w '%{http_code}\n'

The port is on 127.0.0.1, for this machine alone. Next: share it with the LAN, or send the whole machine through dotdash.

items.title: The subscription
items.text: The client fetches the subscription every subscription_interval seconds (an hour), through dotdash, so it stays current where only dotdash gets through, such as through a relay while only some addresses do. When that fails, as on a first start, it fetches directly. It asks the URL for the device's Xray config, the one client-config --full prints, and takes its outbounds; when they changed and Xray accepts them, it restarts Xray on them. It keeps the last ones Xray accepted, so a restart while the URL is out of reach starts on them. Relays in the subscription are outbounds like the others: while only a relay gets through, the client goes through it.

items.title: Share the proxy port
items.text:
The proxy port, 7890, is SOCKS5 and HTTP on one port. At first it listens on 127.0.0.1, for this machine alone, and asks for nothing. To let other devices on the LAN use it, publish it on an address they can reach. Devices then have to give a username and a password: dotdash and the generated proxy_password secret.

Note

192.168.1.10 below stands for this machine's LAN address: use yours.

  1. Find this machine's LAN address, the one devices reach it at:

    hostname -I     # this machine's addresses, such as 192.168.1.10

  2. Publish the port on that address:

    sudo morzer config set listen=192.168.1.10

    Or on every address of this machine with listen=0.0.0.0, which keeps working if the address changes but also publishes the port on any other network the machine is on. Allow 7890/tcp from the LAN if the machine has a firewall.

  3. Print the settings devices need:

    sudo morzer task run proxy-config --output

    For devices on the network (as secret as a password):
socks5h://dotdash:<password>@192.168.1.10:7890
http://dotdash:<password>@192.168.1.10:7890

Or, for an app that asks for them apart: server 192.168.1.10, port 7890,
username dotdash, password <password>.

    With listen=0.0.0.0 the task can't tell which address devices use, so give it after --: proxy-config --output -- 192.168.1.10.

A new password, which every device then needs:

sudo morzer secret rotate proxy_password
sudo morzer task run proxy-config --output

Back to this machine alone: sudo morzer config unset listen.

Beyond 127.0.0.1 the password can't be turned off: an open proxy on a LAN serves whoever else gets on it.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Set one with sudo morzer config set <name>=<value>; edit a rules parameter with sudo morzer config edit <name>.

Name Default listen 127.0.0.1 the address the proxy port is published on; anything but 127.0.0.1 asks devices for proxy_user and proxy_password (sharing) port 7890 the SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy port geoip empty a geoip.dat in place of Xray's own, as <url> <sha256> (other geodata) geosite empty a geosite.dat in place of Xray's own, as <url> <sha256> proxy_user dotdash the username devices give beyond 127.0.0.1 direct_rules a comment destinations reached around dotdash, one rule per line (rules) block_rules a comment destinations refused, one rule per line proxy_rules a comment destinations sent through dotdash even when a direct rule matches them too, one rule per line subscription_interval 3600 seconds between fetches of the subscription probe_url https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 what picking the fastest link and the health check fetch through dotdash cdn use skip: links through a CDN are never picked nor probed; only a subscription with nothing else still sends traffic to one. A dotdash server of 0.13.0 or later tells a relay's CDN links apart ipv6 allow block: every IPv6 destination refused before any other rule, a direct rule's included, so apps fall back to IPv4; with tun it is still taken in, so nothing leaves around dotdash gateway false under tun, this machine is its LAN's gateway, and doctor checks the host for it (gateway) dns_listen none under tun, the address and port that answers the LAN's DNS, such as 192.168.1.10:53 dns_server 1.1.1.1 under tun, the DNS server asked directly, around dotdash, for dotdash's server names, the direct rules and the LAN's own names (tun)

Profiles (installation.profile): tun, the whole machine.

items.title: Secrets
items.text: Name Generated subscription_url no the device's subscription URL, as the server's client-config prints it proxy_password yes the password devices give beyond 127.0.0.1

items.title: Tasks
items.text: Task proxy-config --output [-- <address>] the proxy URLs and credentials devices need; the address only with listen=0.0.0.0

items.title: Health
items.text: doctor and each apply fetch probe_url through dotdash, and with gateway=true check that the host forwards the LAN into TUN.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
Everything goes through dotdash unless a rule says otherwise. Three parameters hold the rules, checked in this order:

  • block_rules: destinations refused;
  • proxy_rules: destinations sent through dotdash, even when a direct rule matches them too, such as one site out of a list that otherwise goes around dotdash;
  • direct_rules: destinations reached directly, around dotdash.

Each holds rules in the apps' classical form without the target, one per line, with # for comments:

# around dotdash
DOMAIN-SUFFIX,example.net
IP-CIDR,192.168.0.0/16
Rule Matches DOMAIN,<name> that name alone DOMAIN-SUFFIX,<name> the name and every name under it DOMAIN-KEYWORD,<word> names that contain the word DOMAIN-REGEX,<expression> names the regular expression matches GEOSITE,<list> names on a list of Xray's geosite data, such as category-ads-all IP-CIDR,<range>, IP-CIDR6,<range> addresses in the range GEOIP,<list> addresses on a list of Xray's geoip data, such as private DST-PORT,<port> that port, or a range such as 8000-9000

A line of another type stops the change: morzer says which line.

Edit them in an editor, or set them from a file:

sudo morzer config edit direct_rules
sudo morzer config set --set-file direct_rules=rules.txt

items.title: Other geodata
items.text:
GEOSITE and GEOIP rules name lists in Xray's own geosite.dat and geoip.dat. Lists of your choice need those files from elsewhere: give geosite (or geoip) a URL and the file's sha256: a pinned version rather than one that changes, with no login or query in the URL, which the client's log would show:

curl -sL <url> | sha256sum
sudo morzer config set geosite="<url> <sha256>"

The client fetches the file through dotdash once it runs, within a minute, tests the rules on it, keeps it, and restarts on it; its log says geosite.dat: fetched. Add the rules that name its lists then: until it is there, Xray has its own file, which lacks them. A client that has such rules and no file yet, as after a reinstall, fetches it at start, once, directly, where it can: not under tun, whose kill switch stops it, so unset those rules until the file is back. A fetched file replaces Xray's own entirely, so every list a rule names has to be in it. Unset, the client is back on Xray's own.

items.title: IP rules match addresses, not names
items.text: An IP rule matches only an address an app gives. A name is never looked up to match one, so this machine's resolver never learns the names that go through dotdash. no-resolve, which older rules carry, changes nothing.

items.title: When dotdash is out of reach
items.text:
With no links at all, as on a first start that can't fetch the subscription, everything but the direct rules is refused: nothing leaves around dotdash by accident.

When every link failed its last check, as just after the server was down, traffic takes the subscription's first link rather than waiting up to two minutes for the next check, so the client carries traffic again as soon as the server is back. With a standby relay, its links come first and are never checked: the client goes through it only then.

items.title: The whole machine
items.text:
The tun profile sends every connection on the machine through dotdash, with no proxy settings: its Docker containers' and IPv6 included. The proxy port and the rules stay as they are.

sudo morzer config set installation.profile=tun
sudo morzer config unset installation.profile     # back to the proxy port alone

  • DNS answers with fake addresses, and the names go to dotdash, which resolves them. dns_server (1.1.1.1), asked directly, answers only for dotdash's server names, the direct rules, and .lan, .local and .home.arpa names. Set it to your router's address for the LAN's own names, or where public resolvers don't answer:

    sudo morzer config set dns_server=192.168.1.1

  • With dotdash out of reach, nothing gets out around it. Nor while Xray itself is down, after a crash or on the restart for a new subscription: a kill switch keeps routing rules that let only Xray's own connections and the LAN out then. sudo morzer doctor checks they are in place.

  • Networks the machine is directly on, such as its LAN, stay reachable directly.
  • The subscription and the dotdash server must be reachable over the machine's main interface, as they normally are.

Xray then runs as root with NET_ADMIN, DAC_OVERRIDE and NET_BIND_SERVICE, on the host's network, with /dev/net/tun: a TUN interface takes nothing less. Its root filesystem stays read-only. The kill switch runs beside it as root with NET_ADMIN alone. Leaving the profile, or stopping dotdash-client, takes its rules out. If it was killed instead and the machine reaches nothing but its LAN, take them out by hand:

sudo ip rule del pref 9001; sudo ip rule del pref 9002
sudo ip -6 rule del pref 9001; sudo ip -6 rule del pref 9002

items.title: A gateway for the LAN
items.text:
Under tun, the machine can be its LAN's gateway: devices whose gateway is its address go through dotdash too, with nothing to set up on them.

It is a gateway beside the main router, on the same LAN: one network interface, and the main router keeps the internet link and hands out addresses. It doesn't replace the router. Making this machine the LAN's only router, with two interfaces, its own DHCP server and NAT, is host setup that dotdash leaves to you; a router system such as OpenWrt suits that better.

It carries IPv4 only. IPv6 from the LAN can't go through it, so step 4 turns IPv6 off around it, before any device is pointed at it.

Note

192.168.1.10 below stands for this machine's LAN address (hostname -I shows it): use yours.

  1. Turn it on, so doctor checks the host for it:

    sudo morzer config set gateway=true

  2. Let the host forward. It must forward IPv4:

    echo net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-dotdash-gateway.conf
sudo sysctl --system

    Docker sets the host's FORWARD policy to DROP on many machines, which drops the LAN's traffic before TUN sees it (dropped, never sent around dotdash). Two rules in Docker's DOCKER-USER chain let it through:

    sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER -o Meta -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER -i Meta -j ACCEPT

    They don't outlive a reboot by themselves: add them to whatever restores the host's firewall, or to a systemd unit that runs after docker.service. doctor names whichever is missing.

  3. Answer the LAN's DNS, if devices are to ask this machine:

    sudo morzer config set dns_listen=192.168.1.10:53

    Not 0.0.0.0:53, which clashes with systemd-resolved's stub.

  4. Turn IPv6 off around it. A main router that advertises IPv6 gives every device a second way out, straight past this machine. Turn off IPv6, or its router advertisements, on the main router; failing that, on each device. Then check on this machine:

    ip -6 route show default     # prints nothing once the main router stops advertising

    A line with proto ra there means the LAN still has IPv6 from the main router.

  5. Point devices at it: hand out 192.168.1.10 as the gateway (and DNS server) from the main router's DHCP, or set it on each device.

  6. Check from a device: an IP checker shows the dotdash exit, and an IPv6 test (curl -6 https://api6.ipify.org) fails rather than showing the device's own address.

items.title: Changelog
items.text:
All notable changes to this project are documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • client-config's Xray config answers devices' DNS with fake DNS, as dotdash-client's TUN does: a name gets a stand-in address at once and the server looks it up, so a first visit to a name no longer waits for a lookup through the tunnel (53 ms less in the lab). dns_resolver is now the server's alone.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• A relay can go through other relays instead of the servers: via takes their lines as relay-entry prints them, reached by REALITY or, with via_link=xhttp, XHTTP through their own sites. The servers never see its address, for a relay on an address worth keeping. The manager's roster takes both.

  • standby at the end of a relay's line in relays keeps that relay idle while others get through: devices get its links last, and their Xray configs, dotdash-client's included, don't check them and use them only once every other link fails. The manager's roster takes standby on a relay.

  • A direct line in upstreams makes the server's own address a way out, for a server already on a residential line: alone, or beside proxies as their backup or fallback. doctor asks it from the server itself.

  • dotdash-manager adopt takes a running server's keys and its devices' ids, so a network set up by hand moves under the manager without devices getting new links or subscription URLs.

  • dotdash-manager join prints a script to pipe over ssh, and joined keeps the id and key it prints back. Nothing goes into the roster by hand, and a machine installed already is only pointed at the manager.

  • dotdash-client's proxy_rules send destinations through dotdash even when a direct rule matches them too, such as one site out of a geosite list that otherwise goes around it. Block rules still come first.

  • dotdash-client's geoip and geosite take other geodata, as <url> <sha256>, for rules naming lists Xray's own lacks. The client fetches the file through dotdash once it runs, keeps it, and restarts on it.

  • A relay's xhttp via leg takes via_fingerprint, the TLS client hello it shows the relay it goes through. none drops the browser mimicry for Xray's own TLS stack, which looks like a server fetching from another rather than a phone; the default, chrome, is unchanged. The manager's roster takes it.

items.title: Added
items.text: • dotdash-client's cdn=skip leaves links through a CDN out: the client never picks one, nor probes it. Telling a relay's CDN links apart needs a dotdash server of 0.13.0 or later.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • In devices' Xray configs, a relay's CDN outbounds are named dotdash-cdn-relay-<n>-<m> (was dotdash-relay-<n>-cdn-<m>) and come after every other outbound, so traffic the balancer can't place goes to a CDN only when there is no other link.

items.title: Added
items.text: • A relay's CDN links take a path of their own (the relay's new cdn_xhttp_path, cdnpath= on its line in relays), so a CDN in front never learns the path devices reach the relay by directly, and look less like a tunnel to it: session, sequence and padding in cookies, no event-stream type.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • CDN links upload at most 8 KiB per request instead of 32 KiB. Base64-encoded into headers, 32 KiB came to about 44 KB, past the 20 KB or so of headers CDN edges take, so any larger upload got a 431 and broke its connection.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
• cdn-check no longer reports a CDN as serving subscriptions when an app behind the site (cover) answers every path: it now knows its decoy by the decoy's contents, and calls a 2xx without them refused.

  • A relay's XHTTP path drops the client address a CDN in front passes on in X-Real-IP or CF-Connecting-IP, as the server's does, so it no longer reaches the relay's Xray.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • A relay with a site of its own serves devices' subscriptions under its own domain alone. A CDN in front that strips the headers saying it passed a request on is refused too, once it sends another name as Host, such as its own; cdn-check tells.

items.title: Added
items.text: • A relay's name parameter: a label that devices' links through it carry in place of relay <n>, such as edge-1 · reality. relay-entry ends the relay's line with name=, and a name an earlier relay took goes by the number.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • Links are named <route> · <transport>, such as server · reality, relay 2 · hy2 or relay · cdn, without the device's name, which an app showed on every link. Apps pick up the names at the next subscription refresh; hand-imported links keep the old ones, and outbound tags are unchanged.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • The server's relay-config prints the relay's dotdash_xhttp_path before the dotdash_link=xhttp-reality that needs it. In the old order the relay switched to XHTTP with no path, failed its health check and stayed cut off until morzer gave up.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• A relay with a site of its own serves Hysteria2 too, under that site's certificate (installation.profile=own-site,hysteria2, UDP hysteria2_port, 443). Its relay-entry line ends with hy2=<port>, and devices get a <device> | hy2 | relay link and outbound through it.

  • A device's subscription names itself after the server's exit, its country's flag and IPv4 address (Profile-Title), so the apps that show a name (Happ, Hiddify) show where traffic leaves instead of the server's domain. The server asks every ten minutes, through the upstreams (exit_ipv4_url, exit_info_url).

  • dotdash-manager gives a canary watching a relay with Hysteria2 the relay's port (dotdash_hysteria2_port), so the canary's hysteria2 profile checks it, and a relay whose Hysteria2 its canaries can't get through loses that link (off=hysteria2).

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• Links are named <device> | <transport>, with | relay, | cdn or | relay, cdn through a relay or a CDN, numbered where there are several (relay 1, cdn 2), and | server <n> with several servers, in place of the host names they used to carry: an app shows no relay, CDN or server name.

  • The server's gate probes each upstreams line every 10 s instead of 30. When a line goes silent, new connections move to another after about 8 s on average and 12 at most, instead of 18 and 31.

  • dotdash-manager sync and rotate swap read the machines' facts eight at a time instead of one after another, so a fleet of many machines syncs in a fraction of the time.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
• Under the metrics profile, a change of a secret after morzer restart xray restarts Xray again instead of failing: the exporters reach Xray's and the gate's metrics on an internal network of their own rather than sharing their network namespaces, which a recreate left them stranded in. The same holds on the relay.

  • A device's subscription through an own-site relay serves its links again. The relay's Caddy passed the request on with a Via header, which the server takes for a CDN's, so the server answered with its site, and apps reported a config they could not parse.

  • The relay's cover-site health check checks its own site under the own-site profile: that Caddy is healthy and the app cover names answers. It used to report the profile off and pass, so config set cover= was never undone when the site could not reach the app.

  • dotdash-manager runs one at a time on its state, and a second run waits. Two overlapping runs, such as a timer's sync during a rotate, could lose each other's changes. The state is synced to disk before it replaces the old one, and sync --dry-run no longer writes it.

  • dotdash-manager sync judges a relay only by canary readings within 90 minutes of the newest. A canary that went quiet used to hold a relay up with an old success while another canary found it blocked.

  • bootstrap.sh installs morzer 0.18.0, which dotdash 0.9.0 needs, instead of 0.17.0. On Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 11, which ship no minisign, it installs minisign's own release, checked against a pinned sum, where it used to stop at "Unable to locate package minisign".

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • dotdash-client carries traffic again as soon as the server is back from an outage. When every link failed its last check, traffic now takes the subscription's first link instead of being refused for up to two minutes until the next check. With no links yet, it is still refused.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• An upstreams proxy line tagged warm=<n> keeps n connections to its proxy open and logged in (the warm profile), so a new connection skips the proxy's handshake. From a server 34 ms from its proxy, a fetch's first byte came after 51 ms instead of 203 ms.

  • An app on Apple's network stack, by its User-Agent, gets the subscription's links with Safari's TLS hello (fp=safari), as its platform sends; every other app keeps Chrome's.

  • When REALITY fails, a canary's facts say what stops it from its own network (blocked_by: ip, sni, tls or freeze), and dotdash-manager names it in its verdicts. With ipv6_url set, facts also say per transport whether the server carries IPv6 (ipv6).

  • A canary's facts say per transport whether the server carries devices' UDP (udp), by asking a DNS server (udp_target) over UDP through each. The leaks page says what WebRTC shows in each mode, and how to stop a browser on a proxy port leaking the device's address.

  • A canary also tries REALITY with its ClientHello split into TLS records (reality_split in its facts). When only that gets through, dotdash-manager sets the server's hello_split, or puts split on a relay's line, so devices' Xray configs split their REALITY hello past a block on the name by SNI.

  • dotdash-manager rotate start, swap and finish rotate the servers' REALITY key with no device cut off. The canaries watching servers prove the next key before devices and relays move to it. A canary's facts now name the key it checks under.

  • The server can accept a second REALITY key beside reality_key (reality_second_key, with the reality_key_second and reality_short_id_second secrets), so the key can be rotated with no device cut off. The docs walk through the three steps.

  • The server's and the relay's metrics profile writes Xray's traffic per inbound and outbound, its upstreams' or servers' verdicts and its heap into the node exporter's textfile directory beside morzer's own metrics, never per device.

  • dotdash-manager report shows how long each path of each server and relay lasted before it was first blocked, and the median per path. A server or relay in the roster can carry your own provider and address_since, and the report adds up lifetimes per provider, kept for machines taken out of the roster.

  • A relay can reach the servers over XHTTP with REALITY (dotdash_link=xhttp-reality), connections reused across devices: about 100 ms sooner to a page's first byte, for about twice the CPU. relay-config prints the settings and the dotdash_xhttp_path secret when the server runs xhttp-reality.

  • The canary's hysteria2 profile checks a server's Hysteria2 beside REALITY, on dotdash_hysteria2_port (443), logging in as the canary's own id, in measure and facts too. A server under hysteria2 tells canary-config and dotdash-manager its port, and the manager sets it on the canaries watching that server.

  • The server's hysteria2 profile: Hysteria2 on UDP 443 (hysteria2_port), under the site's own certificate, each device's UUID its login. Devices get a [hy2] link and an outbound. It runs BBR, or Brutal at hysteria2_up Mbit/s for devices that ask.

  • A canary's facts time each path that gets through (latency_ms) and its own network without dotdash (direct_ms). dotdash-manager report ends with each server's and relay's median per path beside its canaries' network, and what each relay adds over the servers.

  • dotdash-client's dns_server (1.1.1.1): under tun, the DNS server asked directly for dotdash's server names, the direct rules and .lan, .local and .home.arpa names. Your router's address answers the LAN's own names.

  • An upstreams line can put its tags first, name=isp-a group=ipv6 | socks5://…, so each name stays at the start of its line however long the URL runs. Lines with the tags after the URL still work, and a line without tags is still just its URL.

  • Each device's subscription URL also serves its Xray config, the one client-config --full prints, to a request with Accept: application/json alone, and at the URL with .json: for a client that runs Xray itself. Own-site relays pass it on; a request a CDN passed on gets the site's 404.

  • dotdash-manager report: how long each server and relay lasted before it first burnt, how often and how long it was burnt, which paths went off and how often a spare stood in, with the relays' median lifetime; relays taken out of the roster stay in it.

  • Spare relays: a relay with spare = true in dotdash-manager's roster runs and is watched but devices don't get it, until a relay burns; then it stands in for that relay, in its pools, at the next sync, and waits again once the relay is back.

  • A canary's facts also catch a freeze counted on what the device sends: each transport uploads 64 KB to freeze_up_url, and one whose upload gets no answer for 8 seconds twice counts as not getting through, named under stalled_up. freeze_up_url=none turns it off.

  • dotdash-manager tells a burnt relay that's blocked from one that's down, by the relay's own hourly fleet row: running means blocked on the way, so replace its address; a row gone quiet or services down means fix the machine first.

  • A canary's facts catch a connection frozen after its first 16-20 KB: each transport also downloads freeze_url (64 KB), and one whose download stops partway twice counts as not getting through, with the bytes it got under stalled. freeze_url=none turns it off.

  • dotdash-manager drops just a relay's blocked path when its canaries find one transport cut while another gets through: the relay's line gets off=reality, off=xhttp or off=mkcp, and devices get its other links. A path blocked on every relay is kept and reported.

  • A server or relay can share a machine with your own web server on 80 and 443, which passes dotdash's names through untouched. listen, https_port and http_port choose where dotdash publishes, such as spare ports on 127.0.0.1; the server's entry_port keeps links on 443.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• The server's gate, the relay and the warm container probe each connection's path MTU and hold at most 128 KiB unsent per connection. A path that silently drops large packets no longer stalls every TCP link (Vision's first byte 332 ms instead of never), and a click waits less behind a download on XHTTP.

  • Every TCP link in a device's Xray config, and the relay's link to its server, gives up a connection after 15 s of unacknowledged data and redials. When a censor freezes a connection, XHTTP answers again after 17 s instead of a minute.

  • A Hysteria2 connection a network froze is given up after 15 s of silence instead of 30, and the device reconnects: it answers again after 16 s instead of 31. The Xray config devices get sends keepalives, so a healthy connection idle that long stays open.

  • The gate times out an upstreams line's probe after 1.5 s (Xray's burst observatory) rather than 5. A line throttled hard but still answering, which added a second to every connection, now counts as down and the next one carries the traffic.

  • When no upstreams line answers its probe, the gate sends connections through the first line instead of failing them, so a wrong verdict, or a single line that is only slow, no longer stops the traffic. Nothing leaves directly.

  • Every apply, update and doctor refuses upstream_udp=true while an upstreams line is an HTTP or HTTPS proxy, which drops UDP. The policy check also reads a line's group= and kind when name= and group= come before its URL.

  • The Xray config devices get (client-config --full, the subscription's JSON, dotdash-client) shares UDP flows over a few connections on REALITY links (XUDP Mux): one connection for 20 flows instead of 20, each later flow answering in one round trip instead of three.

  • The DNS tunnel sends every 50 ms (xdns_tti), not every 200: about three times the speed. Devices' configs spread its queries over three resolvers (xdns_resolvers), so each sees little more than before.

  • Hysteria2 no longer answers a stray packet with a stateless reset, which the site's own HTTP/3 never sends and a prober could tell apart.

  • Devices' and relays' configs probe each link at a moment of its own (burstObservatory), not all together, which tied a device's links to each other for an observer. Picking the fastest works as before.

  • Every Xray container sets Go's soft memory limit (GOMEMLIMIT) at about 90% of its memory cap, so Go collects garbage harder near the cap instead of the kernel killing Xray.

  • The server's gate and a relay send to devices on BBR, in their own containers only (tcp_congestion). On a lossy last mile it kept 6-50 times cubic's speed in the lab. Set tcp_congestion=cubic on a kernel without tcp_bbr, where the apply would otherwise fail and roll back.

  • A server that resolves names itself (resolve=gateway), and the Xray config client-config prints, answer a name looked up before from the cache at once, even after it expired, and ask again in the background, for a day at most. A site revisited no longer waits for a lookup through the upstream.

  • dotdash-client runs Xray instead of mihomo. It asks the subscription URL for the device's Xray config and uses whichever outbound answers fastest. Update the server first: an older one serves no config, and the client then refuses traffic rather than send it around dotdash.

  • dotdash-client's rule parameters keep their form. A line whose type isn't DOMAIN, DOMAIN-SUFFIX, DOMAIN-KEYWORD, DOMAIN-REGEX, GEOSITE, IP-CIDR, IP-CIDR6, GEOIP or DST-PORT stops the change, naming the line. IP rules never look a name up, so no-resolve changes nothing.

  • The server and the relay need morzer 0.18.0. Before an apply starts them, it checks each port they publish on that port's own address and protocol, the UDP ports of the DNS tunnel, mKCP and Hysteria2 included, and refuses to start with one taken, naming it, rather than failing after the old containers stopped.

  • dotdash-acme-dns needs morzer 0.17.1, which backs up a machine set up without a recovery key, so updates there no longer depend on the placeholder secret the bundle carried; the secret is gone.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • dotdash-client under tun no longer sends traffic around dotdash while Xray is down, after a crash or on the restart for a new subscription. A kill switch keeps routing rules that let only Xray's own connections and the LAN out then, and doctor checks them.

items.title: Added
items.text: • The dotdash-acme-dns bundle runs your own acme-dns server for cert_issuer=acme-dns, installed with morzer like the other bundles. Its register task prints each parent domain's CNAME and the acme_dns secret for the machines under it.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • morzer rollback from this release to 0.7.0 works again on the server and the canary, and updates to it may run unattended: only 0.7.0 itself needs its pre-update backup to go back. A canary on 0.6.x is refused the update and set up again from canary-config, as for 0.7.0.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• cert_issuer=acme-dns on the server and the own-site relay takes a wildcard certificate over the domain's parent through a DNS-01 check handed to acme-dns by one CNAME (the acme_dns secret), keeping the machine's own name out of the certificate logs. Keep servers and relays under separate parents.

  • direct=false keeps every server's address out of devices' links, configs and subscriptions: devices reach the servers only through relays and CDN hosts, and fetch subscriptions only through own-site relays. dotdash-manager sets it on every server from the roster's direct.

  • A cdn-check task on the server tells whether each CDN in front of it and of its relays is refused a subscription, by fetching a decoy one, with no links in it, through each.

  • cover on the server and the own-site relay puts your own app behind the cover site, by its URL: Caddy passes it every request but a subscription's, XHTTP's and those for your own files, and doctor checks that it answers. An app published on a host port is reached as host.docker.internal.

  • An ipv6 parameter on the server, the relay and the client: block keeps IPv6 out. The client refuses it before any rule, the relay drops it, and the server resolves names to IPv4 only and blocks IPv6 addresses, so dual-stack sites still work over IPv4.

  • upstream_mode decides how the upstreams share the traffic: failover, the first line that answers, then the fastest of the rest; fastest; or balance, connections spread over every line that answers. upstream_pin puts a named line first.

  • The wireguard-line task turns a WireGuard exit's wg-quick file into its upstreams line, and openvpn-line an OpenVPN exit's client config into its own.

  • Every bundle names what an authority it follows may set: on a server the devices, the shared keys and the server, relay, CDN and pool lists; on a relay the devices and its way to the servers; on a canary its target; on a client its subscription and proxy password. The rest stays the machine's own.

  • A facts task on the server and the relay prints, as JSON, what each tells the authority it follows after every change: a server's domain, ports, public key and encryption string, and a relay's relay-entry line.

  • The canary's facts task tells the authority it follows, before every fleet publish, whether each transport gets through to its target, and, with the new control_url, whether the canary's own network answers without dotdash.

  • dotdash-manager sync leaves a relay out of the servers' relays and pools once every canary watching it got through none of its paths three readings in a row, and brings it back when one gets through. It keeps every relay if all would go at once, and only reports a burnt server.

  • dotdash-manager, installed with uv from the repository's manager/, runs a network from one roster: it makes the servers' shared keys, gives every server and relay the same devices, and keeps relays, canaries and client machines pointed at the servers, each machine following it through morzer's desired state.

  • cdn_only on the relay gives devices its CDN links alone, none to its own address, so a relay can stay the origin of the CDNs in front of it while the relays devices reach directly are blocked. relay-entry marks the line cdn-only.

  • The relay's entry_host parameter, the address devices reach it at, which relay-entry uses when given none; under own-site it is the relay's domain.

  • When nothing gets out, doctor names each upstreams line it asked by its name=: no answer, refused credentials, a WireGuard peer that did not carry it, or an OpenVPN tunnel that is down.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• The server and own-site relays answer a subscription request a CDN passed on with the site's 404, so a device's links never pass through a CDN, which could read them. They recognise one by the headers a CDN adds, such as X-Forwarded-For and Via.

  • Breaking: site_dir is gone from the server and the relay. Your own files are always read from /srv/dotdash (the relay's /srv/dotdash-relay), which a symlink can point elsewhere, so that one parameter, cover, names pages or an app. Move files kept elsewhere before updating.

  • Breaking: every bundle needs morzer 0.17.0, which health-checks a parameter change, undoes it when the check fails, and waits only on the services the change re-creates. Update morzer first: an older one refuses the release and changes nothing.

  • Breaking: the server's healthcheck_url, healthcheck6_url and healthcheck_expect are probe_url, probe6_url and probe_expect, as the other bundles name them. An update drops the old values, so set changed ones again after it.

  • Breaking: every way out is a line of the new upstreams secret, in order: socks5://, socks5+tls://, http:// or https:// proxies, wireguard:// exits and up to 8 openvpn:// exits. Set it before updating, which is refused until it is: sudo morzer secret set upstreams.

  • Breaking: ipv6=separate sends IPv6 destinations through the lines marked group=ipv6 alone, in place of the IPv6 proxy, and a line may serve both groups. upstream_udp now needs every line to carry UDP, tunnels included.

  • Breaking: the canary names its target as the relay does, dotdash_server, dotdash_address, dotdash_port, dotdash_public_key, dotdash_id, dotdash_encryption, dotdash_short_id, and dotdash_ before the XHTTP and mKCP ones. A canary is not updated to it but set up again from canary-config.

  • canary-config also prints the server's mKCP opener, as dotdash_kcp_open.

  • Breaking: the client's dns_listen is off at none, as every other parameter says it, rather than off.

  • morzer rollback from this release of the server or the canary is refused, since the earlier release lacks the new names; the pre-update backup is the way back.

  • The relay's cert_issuer takes effect with config set, without a full apply.

  • The server, the relay and the canary run Xray 26.11.9, and the client mihomo 1.19.34.

items.title: Removed
items.text:
• Breaking: the upstream, upstream6, upstream_backup, upstream_wireguard and upstream_openvpn secrets and the upstream_protocol, upstream6_protocol and upstream_backup_protocol parameters with their *_tls ones. Their ways out become lines of upstreams.

  • Breaking: the relay's deprecated dotdash_server. dotdash_servers is now required: on a relay that still has only dotdash_server, set dotdash_servers before updating.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• CDNs in front of a relay: with the own-site profile, the relay's new cdn_hosts parameter adds cdn=<names> to its line, and devices get an XHTTP link through each CDN, shaped as for the server's cdn_hosts. The CDN's account then names a relay rather than the server, and pools take these names too.

  • A QUIC-shaped opener in front of mKCP: the new kcp_open parameter (quic) sends a QUIC-Initial-shaped packet before the flow, on the server, relays and canary; links carry it in fm= for v2rayN and v2rayNG. It is a fixed shape, off unless set, and no help where QUIC itself is blocked; measure it on a canary first.

  • The canary's measure adds throughput: three downloads of the new download_url parameter (1 MB from speed.cloudflare.com unless set, https:// only, none to skip) through each transport, with how many completed and the median Mbit/s.

  • VLESS over mKCP, an opt-in UDP transport for networks that block the TCP ones: the new mkcp profile serves it on kcp_port (8447/udp), encrypted under the new kcp_seed secret, its packets starting with a fake kcp_header (dtls unless set). Devices get a [kcp] link and outbound per server (v2rayN, v2rayNG).

  • mKCP on relays: the relay's mkcp profile serves it under its own kcp_seed, relay-entry adds kcp=<port>,<header>,<seed> to its line, and devices get a [relay <host> kcp] link and outbound through it. A server from before reads no such field.

  • The canary checks mKCP with --profile mkcp, with the server's kcp_port, kcp_header and kcp_seed, which canary-config prints for a server under the mkcp profile; measure reports it beside REALITY.

  • Pools, so a leaked device no longer gives away every relay and CDN host: the new pools parameter lists, per pool, its devices, relay hosts and CDN hosts. A device in a pool gets its pools' entry points and those in no pool; a device in none gets them all, and a member that names nothing is reported.

  • XHTTP through a relay with a site of its own: the site routes a secret path, the new xhttp_path secret, to the relay's Xray, relay-entry adds the path to the relay's line, and client-config and the subscriptions add an [relay … xhttp] link and outbound. The relay needs morzer 0.15.1.

  • A backup proxy for when the upstream fails: upstream_backup_protocol with the new upstream_backup secret. Connections leave through the upstream while the gate's probes get through it, every 30 s, through the backup while they don't, and return by themselves.

  • A relay with a site of its own serves devices their subscriptions inside the restricted network, fetched from the server through its tunnel. client-config prints through the relay <domain>: https://<domain>/<token> under the server's URL, and relay-entry ends such a relay's line with own-site.

  • Local CDNs, for restricted networks: with their names in the new cdn_hosts parameter, client-config, the Xray config and the subscriptions add an XHTTP link through each, uploading in GET requests with the data in headers, as such CDNs need. The CDN page covers the setup and the risks.

  • A relay can serve a site of its own: with a domain pointing at it and the new own-site profile, devices send the relay's own name, and a prober meets a real site with a certificate for that name, so the name and the address agree as for any site. relay-config offers it first; a borrowed site (site) still works.

  • The upstream can be a WireGuard exit: upstream_protocol=wireguard takes the wg-quick client config in the new upstream_wireguard secret, such as a home router's or a VPN provider's, and the gate runs Xray's own WireGuard with no extra privilege. It carries UDP, and IPv6 when the exit has it.

  • The upstream can be an OpenVPN exit: upstream_protocol=openvpn with the new openvpn profile takes the client config in the new upstream_openvpn secret, and a new config takes effect when set. Its container drops its default route before OpenVPN starts, so nothing leaves around the tunnel.

  • A tunnel's config has a secret of its own, so it is set while the proxy is still the upstream, and the switch never leaves the gate without a working upstream: one config set for WireGuard, the profile and then the protocol for OpenVPN.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• The server's and relays' sites answer under any name, so a CDN in front works on its defaults: no Host header to set at the provider. A CDN that sends its own name as SNI gets the site's certificate rather than a failed handshake.

  • Links list XHTTP before REALITY, for each server and each relay, in client-config and the subscriptions: an app tends to try the first link, and REALITY over raw TCP is blocked most often.

  • Subscriptions are served with Cache-Control: no-store, so nothing between the server and a device keeps a copy.

  • The server bundle is published as ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server, and ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash gets no new versions. Switch with sudo morzer update oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server:stable, and point update.channel there if set. The product, its paths and data stay dotdash.

  • The server needs morzer 0.15.1: update morzer before updating dotdash.

  • The upstream secret is no longer required: an installation whose upstream is a tunnel needs none. With a proxy, the egress health check still fails, naming it, while it is unset.

items.title: Removed
items.text: • The xdns-xhttp-reality profile, deprecated since 0.5.0: a server still set to it must switch before updating. xdns,xhttp-reality deploys the same: sudo morzer config set installation.profile=xdns,xhttp-reality.

items.title: Deprecated
items.text: • The xdns-xhttp-reality profile goes in 0.6.0, not in this patch release as 0.5.0 announced: removing it would break a server still set to it. xdns,xhttp-reality deploys the same; switch before 0.6.0 with sudo morzer config set installation.profile=xdns,xhttp-reality.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • The command relay-config prints for the relay machine's last step, relay-entry, now includes --output; without it morzer ran the task and showed nothing, not the line the relays parameter needs.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Every bundle ships the key it is signed with, so morzer init needs no --signing-key: it prints the key, trusts it, and requires every later release to be signed by it. --signing-key still checks even the first release against the repository's.

  • A relay for networks that let only some addresses through: dotdash-relay, a new bundle released with dotdash, carries devices from a machine inside that network on to this server over port 443. The relay-config task prints its setup; its line in the new relays parameter adds a link through it for every device.

  • A client for a Linux machine or a network: dotdash-client, a new bundle released with dotdash, runs mihomo from one device's subscription URL, refreshed through dotdash, with a SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy port, block and direct rules, and a password once the port is published beyond the machine.

  • dotdash-client's tun profile sends every connection on the machine through dotdash with no proxy settings, its containers' and IPv6 included, with DNS answered by fake addresses whose names dotdash resolves; nothing gets out around dotdash when it is out of reach.

  • Under tun, dotdash-client can be its LAN's gateway: devices that use it as theirs go through dotdash too. gateway=true has doctor check that the host forwards the LAN into TUN, naming the two DOCKER-USER rules a FORWARD policy of DROP needs, and dns_listen answers the LAN's DNS.

  • mihomo connects over REALITY and XHTTP with REALITY: those links now carry support-x25519mlkem768=true, without which mihomo leaves out the key share Xray's REALITY requires and fails with "REALITY authentication failed". Other clients pass over the parameter.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• Every bundle of this release needs morzer 0.15.0: run sudo morzer self-update before updating. An older manager refuses the release and changes nothing.

  • The DNS tunnel and XHTTP with REALITY run together as installation.profile=xdns,xhttp-reality, two profiles combined.

  • upstream6 is no longer generated as a placeholder: a fresh install has none until the IPv6 proxy is turned on. An existing value is kept.

  • Unattended updates apply releases again, and morzer rollback works again, both of which 0.4.0 turned off for its own change of the upstream settings. An update from 0.3.x is still refused until the upstream secret is set.

  • bootstrap.sh is served from the documentation site: curl -fsSLO https://morzecrew.github.io/dotdash/bootstrap.sh. The documentation itself moved from the README to https://morzecrew.github.io/dotdash/, one version per release.

items.title: Deprecated
