items.text: • The xdns-xhttp-reality profile: xdns,xhttp-reality deploys the same. It goes in the next release.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • bootstrap.sh installs morzer 0.15.0, which the bundles require. It installed 0.13.0, so init on a freshly prepared host refused the release until morzer self-update.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• The upstream proxy is one secret, upstream, holding user:pass@host:port, so changing proxy is one restart; upstream_host, upstream_port, upstream_username and upstream_password no longer work. Run sudo morzer secret set upstream before updating: an update without it is refused.

  • This release is never applied unattended, and morzer rollback from it is refused, since 0.3.x could not start without the old settings; the pre-update backup is the way back.

  • The IPv6 proxy is the upstream6 secret in the same form, turned on by upstream6_protocol (socks or http, now none by default) instead of upstream6_host. With it on, set upstream6 and upstream6_protocol before updating, or IPv6 goes back to the first proxy.

  • Links are named after the device and transport, such as phone [reality], phone [xhttp] and phone [xhttp+reality], in place of dotdash-phone, dotdash-xhttp-phone and dotdash-xhttp-reality-phone. Apps show the new names once the links are added again, or at the next subscription refresh.

  • With subscriptions on, client-config prints each device's subscription URL alone, so the output stays short; --full before the device's name (-- --full phone) adds its links and Xray config, as before. With subscriptions off it prints what it always did.

  • The subscription service reports healthy only once every device's subscription is written: an apply or an update waits for it, and doctor names the service when that never happens.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Optional subscriptions (subscription): each device gets a URL on the cover site that serves its links, which client-config prints and the app refreshes by itself, so a revocation or a key rotation reaches devices without resending links. Rotating subscription_key moves every URL.

  • An optional second proxy for IPv6 (upstream6_host, with its own credentials), for an upstream that leaves over IPv4 only: destinations with an IPv6 address, sites with both included, leave through it, and the rest through the first. Neither falls back to the other, and doctor names the one that fails.

items.title: Changed
items.text: • The Xray config client-config prints checks all its entries at once every 30 seconds, where it checked one a minute in turn, so it leaves an entry that stops answering within about half a minute instead of up to several minutes. That is two small requests a minute per entry.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• The exit-check task prints the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses the upstream leaves from, each with its network and country, and says whether IPv6 is unavailable or leaves from another network than IPv4. It changes nothing.

  • Every apply and update, and every doctor, checks the release's invariants against what runs: traffic leaves through the upstream only, every inbound demands a client, and only the bundle's own ports are published, by unprivileged containers. An update that breaks one is rolled back; drift fails doctor.

  • An optional third transport: XHTTP under REALITY instead of TLS, on a port of its own (xhttp_reality_port, 8443). The xhttp-reality profile turns it on, xdns-xhttp-reality with the DNS tunnel; client-config then prints a third link and outbound, and the first two as before.

  • The canary's measure task fetches a URL through each transport N times and prints, as JSON, how many succeeded, timed out or failed, and the latency of those that succeeded.

  • The canary's xhttp-reality profile checks XHTTP with REALITY beside REALITY, on the server's xhttp_reality_port.

  • Both bundles carry signed build provenance, naming the commit and workflow run that built them. Check it with gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash:<version> --owner morzecrew, beside the signature morzer verifies.

  • With several servers (servers), canary-config also prints how to point a canary at each of the others: they share the secrets, so only server and address change.

  • The Xray config client-config prints answers the device's DNS, in an app's VPN or TUN mode, over DNS-over-HTTPS (dns_resolver) through the tunnel, with IPv4 addresses only: lookups no longer reach the local network's resolver or need the upstream to relay UDP. The README covers each app.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• Both bundles need morzer 0.14.0 or later. sudo morzer secret edit vless_clients then opens the list as plain text, one client per line, and init needs no --product.

  • When the way out fails, doctor says which layer did: the upstream proxy's address, its credentials, the destination behind it, or an exit that no longer matches healthcheck_expect. The health checks are now cover-site and egress.

  • Xray's log_level defaults to error. At warning and below it names the destinations of failed connections, which a log should not keep; set it back for debugging.

  • client-config prints one complete Xray config per device, for one server too: it uses whichever of REALITY and XHTTP answers fastest on any listed server, and the DNS tunnel only when none answers, instead of printing the tunnel's outbound alone.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
• The cover site's error answers, such as 404 and 405, no longer name the server, and carry the site's headers like its pages do. A prober could tell them apart.

  • The canary's xhttp profile applies. Its Compose file found the base file by a path relative to a directory morzer does not run Compose from, so the profile failed validation.

  • A failed first apply, of dotdash or the canary, no longer leaves a directory where Xray's rendered configuration goes, which made every later apply fail to render it. A missing configuration file or Caddyfile now stops the container from starting instead.

items.title: Security
items.text:
• The upstream no longer learns which hostnames clients visit: this server resolves them over DNS-over-HTTPS sent through the upstream (resolve=gateway, the default) and hands it addresses only. A name resolving to a private address is blocked; resolve=upstream restores the old behaviour.

  • Xray has no route out of the machine. It runs on internal networks only, and a small gate container forwards the public port to it and carries its traffic to the upstream, whose credentials only the gate holds. Whatever Xray's own config says, it cannot send traffic past the upstream.

  • Caddy no longer writes the XHTTP path, a secret, to its log: it logs errors only, and never the request they concern, so no URI, header or client address either. An XHTTP session cut off mid-response used to log all three.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• A morzer bundle for one Docker host, published as ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash: releases as :X.Y.Z and :stable, signed with the release key, and every change to main as :main, signed with the dev key. Requires morzer 0.13.0, Docker 28 and Compose 2.35, or later.

  • REALITY on port 443: a client holding the key reaches Xray over VLESS with Vision, and anything else reaches a Caddy cover site with a Let's Encrypt certificate. https_port moves both to another host port.

  • XHTTP over TLS behind one secret path of the cover site, which also works through a CDN that proxies HTTP/2 to the server.

  • An optional DNS tunnel on UDP/53, VLESS over mKCP with XDNS, for networks where only DNS gets through. The xdns profile turns it on, at install or later; its zone is t.<domain> unless xdns_domain names another.

  • Every inbound uses VLESS Encryption (ML-KEM-768). morzer generates every key, short id and path at install, so no secret is chosen by hand.

  • All client traffic leaves through an upstream SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy you provide, optionally over TLS, with no direct fallback. UDP is relayed only through a SOCKS5 upstream that supports it (upstream_udp).

  • Xray is healthy only while it fetches a URL through the upstream, and doctor fails while it cannot. With healthcheck_expect, a response that does not match, such as a changed exit IP, fails it too.

  • An apply or update succeeds only once port 443 serves the cover site with a certificate a browser trusts.

  • The client-config task prints each device's REALITY and XHTTP links, and the DNS tunnel's outbound when it is on. With servers naming servers that share the keys, it prints links for each and an Xray config that uses whichever answers fastest.

  • One VLESS id per device in vless_clients: deleting a device's line revokes that device alone.

  • The cover site serves your own static files from site_dir wherever they have the requested path, and otherwise a bundled page titled with the server's domain.

  • cert_issuer=internal takes the certificate from Caddy's own CA instead of Let's Encrypt, for a machine the internet cannot reach.

  • Unattended updates: the bundle declares that it keeps no database and is safe to roll back, which morzer requires before it installs a release on its own. Nightly backups include Caddy's certificates.

  • The canary-config task prints the init command and secrets for a dotdash-canary machine acting as one of the clients.

  • dotdash-canary, a second bundle released with dotdash as ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-canary, for a machine inside a network you care about, such as a box at home. It connects to a dotdash server as an ordinary client and needs no open port.

  • The canary's health check fetches probe_url through dotdash over REALITY, and with the xhttp profile also over XHTTP, in up to three tries. doctor fails when all three fail, so a notify target at its default level hears that the network lost its way out.

  • Services run as a non-root user in read-only containers with every capability dropped. Xray's access log is always off.

  • scripts/bootstrap.sh prepares a fresh Debian or Ubuntu server: Docker, sops, age and morzer, unattended security updates, and SSH with keys only once an authorized key exists.

items.title: Releases and CI
items.text:
bundle-ci builds, signs and smoke-tests every pull request and push. A push to main publishes :main; a vX.Y.Z tag publishes all four bundles as :X.Y.Z and :stable, with a GitHub release. Each bundle carries signed build provenance:

gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server:<version> --owner morzecrew

A weekly benchmark measures REALITY and XHTTP under added latency and loss; it informs and never gates. Check a bundle change with morzer release verify ./bundles/server --render-check.

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
This site is Zensical with mike versions on the gh-pages branch. A push to main that touches pages/ publishes dev; a vX.Y.Z tag publishes X.Y and, for the newest minor, moves latest and the root to it.

cd pages && uv run zensical serve    # http://localhost:8047

The diagrams are d2 sources in pages/diagrams, rendered once for the light scheme and once for the dark one into pages/docs/assets/diagrams. The build doesn't run d2: after changing a .d2 file, run pages/diagrams/render.sh and commit the SVGs.

items.title: Relay
items.text: Some networks let only a set list of addresses through, for a region or for mobile data. A device there can't reach a dotdash server outside at all. The dotdash-relay bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay) runs on a machine inside that network, whose address does get through, and carries devices on to the server.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
• Devices connect to the relay on 443 with REALITY, under the name of a site: best, the relay's own, a domain pointing at it and a site it serves (the own-site profile); or a real site next to it, borrowed (its site parameter). To the network, the connection looks like one to that site.
  • Anyone probing the relay's 443 without its keys meets that site: its own, with a certificate for its name, or the borrowed site's real handshake.
  • The relay has keys of its own, and its own copy of the devices allowed in. A device uses the same id as on the server, with a separate link per relay, relay · reality, numbered with several relays (relay 2 · reality) by its place in the server's relays, or named after the relay's name.
  • The relay goes on to the server as one client of its own, a line in the server's vless_clients. With several servers, it uses whichever answers fastest, so a ban on one address doesn't cut it off.
  • It can go through another relay instead (via), so the servers never see its address: Through another relay.
  • Nothing leaves the relay except to dotdash: traffic still exits through the server's upstream proxy.

It can also help where home and mobile lines slow down TLS to faraway hosting: devices then reach only a nearby address, and the relay's own link to the server runs from its hosting network, which the slowdown may not reach.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• The relay's address must get through. Whether one does depends on the network, the provider and the day:
  • host it in a network whose addresses get through, such as a large cloud or hosting provider inside the restricted network. A public list of such subnets is a first filter only, because such lists go stale;
  • test it from each network that matters, on mobile data with Wi-Fi off, before relying on it;
  • run at least two relays, in different networks, so one blocked address costs devices nothing. A spare left installed is moved into place with a DNS change;
  • expect the subnets that get through to shrink, and keep a local CDN as another way in.
  • On those networks only 443 and TCP get through: the DNS tunnel is no use there.
  • Devices need the relay links before restrictions start. An app can't refresh a subscription from the server's site while only some addresses get through, though it can through a relay with a site of its own. See Keep more than one way in.
  • The machine needs Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh), and port 443 free.
  • The official sing-box apps, Karing and NekoBox can't connect to dotdash, relay or not: they lack VLESS Encryption and the key share Xray's REALITY requires.

Next: set one up.

items.title: Set up a relay
items.text: Setting up a relay moves between three places: the dotdash server, the relay machine, and back. The server prints everything the relay needs, and the relay prints the one line the server needs back:

items.title: 1. Pick the site
items.text:
Devices send the name of a site, and anyone probing the relay without its keys meets that site. Two ways:

A site of the relay's own (recommended). A domain whose DNS points at the relay, and the own-site profile: the relay serves a site under that name, with a certificate from Let's Encrypt. To the network the name and the address agree, as they do for any real site. It needs:

  • a domain, relay.example.net, with an A record for the relay's address. Keep relays under a parent of their own, apart from the servers' (a different domain, or *.r.example.net beside the servers' *.s.example.net): a relay's name then tells nothing about the servers, and with a wildcard certificate its own name stays out of the certificate logs;
  • port 80 open as well as 443, for the certificate;
  • in step 3, --domain relay.example.net --profile own-site in place of --set site=….

Your own pages go in /srv/dotdash-relay; without them it serves a plain bundled page titled with the domain. Better still, put an app behind it (cover), as on a server, on the network dotdash-relay_default.

A site next to the relay. No domain needed: the relay borrows the name of a real site, and probes get that site's own handshake. But that name's DNS points at the site, not the relay, and an observer that compares the two can tell. Pick one that is:

  • in the relay's own network, the same hosting provider or nearby, not a big name served from somewhere else;

  • on TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2. curl prints 2 for one that is, and fails for one without TLS 1.3:

    curl -so /dev/null --tlsv1.3 --http2 -w '%{http_version}\n' https://site.example.net

items.title: 2. On the server: a client for the relay
items.text:
Add a <uuid> relay line to vless_clients (uuidgen makes an id), then print the relay's setup:

sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients
sudo morzer task run relay-config --output -- relay

The output is every device's credentials

It carries the relay's copy of vless_clients. Move it to the relay machine as you would a password.

items.title: 3. On the relay: install
items.text:
Install Docker, sops, age and morzer (bootstrap.sh), and make a recovery key as for the server:

morzer secret recipients generate-recovery-key ~/relay-recovery.key   # keep it off the machine

Then run what step 2 printed, with your site and the recovery key's age1… filled in. It has this shape, here with a borrowed site; for a site of the relay's own, replace --set site=… with --domain relay.example.net --profile own-site:

sudo morzer init --release oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay:stable \
  --recovery-recipient age1… \
  --set site=site.example.net \
  --set dotdash_servers=example.com --set dotdash_port=443 \
  --set dotdash_public_key=…
sudo morzer secret set dotdash_id <<'END'          # and dotdash_encryption,
…                                                  # dotdash_short_id,
END                                                # vless_clients
sudo morzer apply

apply succeeds once the relay gets out through dotdash. The relay generates its own keys at init.

items.title: 4. On the relay: its line
items.text:
Give relay-entry the address devices reach the relay at. With a domain, give the domain: links then name it, and moving the relay needs only a DNS change. Without one, give the relay's public IP:

sudo morzer task run relay-entry --output -- relay.example.net   # or 198.51.100.7

It prints one line for the server, its own address, site, public key, short id and encryption, plus the commands a canary needs to check this relay:

198.51.100.7 site.example.net <public key> <short id> <encryption>

Under own-site, the site is the relay's domain, and the line ends with own-site and the relay's XHTTP path. The relay then also serves devices their subscriptions and XHTTP (step 6).

items.title: 5. On the server: add the line to relays
items.text:
One line per relay:

sudo morzer config edit relays

A relay to keep idle while the others get through, such as one on an address worth keeping, gets standby at the end of its line. Devices still get its links, last, but their Xray configs, dotdash-client's included, don't check them, and send traffic through it only once every other link has failed. In an app where you pick a link, pick another while it works.

items.title: 6. Devices
items.text:
client-config now prints a relay · reality link for every device, and the Xray config falls back to the relays when the server itself is out of reach. Under own-site, a relay · xhttp link joins it: XHTTP over TLS behind the relay's site, for networks that block REALITY over raw TCP, the transport blocked most often since early 2026. Subscriptions pick the link up by themselves; otherwise resend the links. Do it now, while devices can still reach the server.

With subscriptions on and a relay under own-site, each device also gets its subscription through the relay:

https://example.com/<token>
through the relay relay.example.net: https://relay.example.net/<token>

Give a device inside the restricted network the second one. The relay fetches it from the server through its own tunnel, so the app keeps refreshing its links while only some addresses get through, and nothing between the relay and the server can read them.

To check, connect a phone on the target network with its relay link alone.

Next: keeping it running.

items.title: Running a relay
items.text: The relay keeps copies of what it got from the server: the devices, and the server's keys. Whatever changes one side has to reach the other.

items.title: Devices
items.text:
A device added to or deleted from the server's vless_clients has to change on the relay too. After the change on the server, relay-config prints the relay's new copy:

# on the server
sudo morzer task run relay-config --output -- relay
# on the relay: the vless_clients block of that output
sudo morzer secret set vless_clients <<'END'
…
END

items.title: Keys
items.text: What changed What to do The server's reality_key, vless_seed or reality_short_id Run relay-config again, and on the relay set dotdash_public_key, dotdash_encryption and dotdash_short_id from it. Until then the relay can't reach the server. The relay's own keys (secret rotate on the relay) Run relay-entry again, replace the relay's line in the server's relays, and send devices their links again (subscriptions pick them up). The relay's address The same: relay-entry -- <new address>, then replace the line.

items.title: A site of its own, later
items.text:
A relay set up with a borrowed site moves to one of its own in place. Point a domain at it and open port 80, then:

sudo morzer config set installation.domains=relay.example.net
sudo morzer config set installation.profile=own-site
sudo morzer task run relay-entry --output -- 198.51.100.7

The site in the line changes and the line gains own-site, so replace the relay's line in the server's relays, and send devices their links again (subscriptions pick them up), with the subscription URL through the relay for those inside the restricted network. sudo morzer config unset installation.profile goes back to the borrowed site.

items.title: Servers
items.text:
The relay goes to every server in dotdash_servers and uses whichever answers fastest. With a new server sharing the keys:

sudo morzer config set dotdash_servers=example.com,b.example.com

Under own-site, sudo morzer apply afterwards: the site fetches subscriptions from these servers, and only an apply restarts it with the new list.

items.title: Through another relay
items.text:
A relay on an address you can't afford to lose can go through another relay instead of to the servers. Its one connection out is then to that relay, which carries it on as one of its devices, and the servers never see its address.

  1. On the server, a client for this relay in vless_clients, and the relay installed from relay-config, as for any relay.
  2. The other relay lets this one in by that client's id. Its copy of vless_clients holds every client but its own: after adding this relay's client on the server, set the other relay's copy again from its own relay-config (Devices).

  3. On the other relay, its line:

    sudo morzer task run relay-entry --output -- <its address>

  4. On this relay, that line in via:

    sudo morzer config edit via

The apply's health check goes through the other relay, and morzer rolls back a line it can't get through. With two lines, it uses whichever relay answers fastest, so one going down doesn't cut it off.

How it reaches the other relay, via_link:

  • reality (the default): REALITY with Vision, one connection for each of its devices' connections, as a device's reality link to a relay.
  • xhttp: XHTTP through the other relay's own site, under that site's certificate, a few connections reused across all its devices, as a device's xhttp link to a relay. To whoever watches this relay, that is a machine fetching from a website, rather than as many connections as its devices make. The other relay needs own-site, and its line then carries own-site <path>, which this one needs.

On the xhttp leg, via_fingerprint sets the TLS client hello this relay shows the other one. The default, chrome, mimics that browser, as the leg has always done. A browser hello between two machines is itself a small tell — an ordinary site is fetched by a server, not a phone — so for a relay that only ever talks to the other relay, none fits better: it drops the browser mimicry and uses Xray's own TLS stack, which looks like a server-side HTTP client. firefox, safari, edge, ios and android pick other browsers, and random a different one per connection. It changes nothing on the reality leg or on the way to the servers.

items.title: Both ways at once
items.text:
While the other relay's address gets through, devices can reach it directly and leave this one idle; once it doesn't, they go through this one. Put both relays' lines in the server's relays, the other relay's first: devices get the other relay's links and this one's, which go through it. A name on each says which is which in the apps, such as name=y on the other relay and name=y-via-x on this one: y · reality, y · xhttp, y-via-x · reality. In apps where you pick a link, pick the other relay's and keep this one's for when they stop working; Xray configs that pick the fastest pick the shorter way while it works, though they check every link every 30 seconds, this one's too.

  • dotdash_servers and the server's keys stay as they are: under own-site, the site still fetches devices' subscriptions from the servers, through the other relay.
  • Or the other relay has no line in the server's relays: then no device gets a link to it and only this relay knows its address, so its firewall can let in this relay alone (with cert_issuer=acme-dns, which needs no port 80). Either way, the server's firewall can let in the relays alone.
  • Each relay on the way adds its round trip to every new connection.
  • dotdash_link=xhttp-reality is a way to the servers only: with via, the link is reality.
  • Devices added on the server go into this relay's copy as before. The other relay's copy needs this relay's client, and its own devices if any.

With the manager, via in the relay's entry of network.toml does all of this.

items.title: Move a relay
items.text:
A relay whose links name its domain moves to a new machine, or a new address, with a DNS change, and devices keep their links. It keeps its keys, which a backup holds. Prepare when you set it up: keep the recovery key off the machine, add a backup target, and set the A record's TTL to 300 s or less.

sudo morzer secret set backup_s3 < ./bucket.yaml   # the bucket's credentials
sudo morzer backup target add s3://bucket/dotdash-relay --credentials backup_s3
sudo morzer backup                                  # one now; each update takes another

Then, on the new machine, after bootstrap.sh:

sudo morzer --product dotdash-relay installation import --from-backup \
  --target s3://bucket/dotdash-relay --credentials-file ./bucket.yaml \
  --identity ~/relay-recovery.key
sudo morzer update oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay:stable

Point the relay's domain at the new address, and open 443, and 80 under own-site. Shut the old machine down: two live relays with one installation id confuse each other's backups. A relay whose links name its IP needs a new line from relay-entry in the server's relays, and new links for devices.

items.title: Watching it
items.text:
doctor and each apply fetch probe_url through dotdash, so they fail when the relay can't reach the server. Have them alert you:

sudo morzer notify target add https://hooks.example/morzer

What the relay can't see is whether devices reach it: only a machine on the networks devices use can. A canary on a mobile line checks the relay as it checks a server, with the commands relay-entry prints.

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
With morzer's own metrics in the node exporter's textfile directory (metrics.textfile), the metrics profile adds the relay's, in the same directory: its traffic per inbound and outbound, and with several servers its verdicts on each. Nothing is counted per device. The exporters run as 65532, so the directory has to be writable by it:

sudo setfacl -m u:65532:rwx /var/lib/prometheus/node-exporter
sudo morzer config set metrics_textfile=/var/lib/prometheus/node-exporter   # its default
sudo morzer config set installation.profile=metrics    # beside own-site or mkcp if you run them
Metric Labels Value dotdash_xray_up role 1 when the exporter read Xray's counters dotdash_inbound_bytes_total role, inbound, direction bytes through an inbound since Xray started dotdash_outbound_bytes_total role, outbound, direction bytes through an outbound since Xray started dotdash_observatory_alive role, outbound 1 when the last check got through a server dotdash_observatory_delay_seconds role, outbound that check's time, while it gets through dotdash_xray_heap_bytes role Xray's Go heap, beside its GOMEMLIMIT

Every series also carries product. rate(dotdash_inbound_bytes_total[5m]) per inbound shows which transport devices use.

items.title: Updates
items.text: As for the server: sudo morzer self-update when a release needs a newer morzer, then sudo morzer update --stage && sudo morzer update --to <version>. Unattended updates follow update.channel=oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-relay:stable; see Operations.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Set one with sudo morzer config set <name>=<value>.

Name Default site none without the own-site profile, a site next to the relay, in its own network, on TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2: devices send its name, and probes get its handshake cover pages with own-site, what the site serves past your own files in /srv/dotdash-relay: pages, the bundled page, or your app's URL, such as http://cover-app:8080 on the network dotdash-relay_default or http://host.docker.internal:8080 cert_issuer acme with own-site, acme (Let's Encrypt, over port 80), acme-dns (a wildcard over a DNS-01 check handed to acme-dns, the acme_dns secret) or internal (Caddy's own CA, for a machine the internet can't reach) entry_host none the address devices reach the relay at, its IP without a domain, for relay-entry with no address and for facts; none under own-site is the relay's domain cdn_hosts none with own-site, the names devices use for local CDNs in front of the relay, comma-separated; relay-entry adds them to the relay's line cdn_only false true: devices get the relay's CDN links alone, none to its own address, so it stays the CDNs' origin; relay-entry ends the line with cdn-only, and refuses it without cdn_hosts name none a label of up to 24 letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores that devices' links through the relay carry in place of relay <n>: edge-1 · reality. relay-entry ends the line with name=; a name an earlier line took goes by the number. Every device's app shows it, so pick one that says nothing about where the relay is hosted dotdash_servers none, given at init the dotdash servers sharing one set of keys, comma-separated domains; the relay uses whichever answers fastest dotdash_port 443 the servers' https_port dotdash_public_key none, given at init the servers' REALITY public key, the pbk of their links dotdash_address none where to connect when dotdash_servers names one server, such as its IP; none reaches each server by its name metrics_textfile /var/lib/prometheus/node-exporter with the metrics profile, the node exporter's textfile directory, writable by 65532 (Metrics) dotdash_link reality how the relay reaches the servers: reality, a REALITY connection with Vision for each device's; xhttp-reality, XHTTP with REALITY on dotdash_xhttp_reality_port, connections reused across devices, about 100 ms sooner to a page's first byte for about twice the CPU here and on the server. Needs the servers' xhttp-reality profile and the dotdash_xhttp_path secret, both of which relay-config prints dotdash_xhttp_reality_port 8443 the servers' xhttp_reality_port, for dotdash_link=xhttp-reality via none other relays to go through instead of the servers, one line each as its relay-entry prints it; with several, whichever answers fastest (Through another relay). Not with dotdash_link=xhttp-reality via_link reality how the relay reaches those in via: reality, REALITY with Vision, a connection for each device's; xhttp, XHTTP through each one's own site under its certificate, connections reused across devices, for which each line has to carry own-site <path>, as relay-entry prints it under own-site via_fingerprint chrome the TLS client hello the xhttp via leg shows the relay it goes through (via_link=xhttp only; the reality leg and the way to the servers are unaffected): chrome, firefox, safari, edge, ios, android mimic that browser; none uses Xray's own Go TLS stack, which looks like a server-side HTTP client rather than a browser; random picks a browser per connection probe_url https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 what the health check fetches through dotdash; any 2xx is healthy tcp_congestion bbr TCP congestion control toward devices, in Xray's own namespace: bbr keeps its pace through a lossy last mile; cubic for a kernel without tcp_bbr. Xray also probes each connection's path MTU and holds at most 128 KiB unsent per connection, and gives its link to a server up after 15 s of unacknowledged data ipv6 allow block: IPv6 destinations end at the relay and never reach a server; names go on https_port 443 host port for REALITY; devices always dial 443, so another is for your own web server passing the relay's name through http_port 80 with own-site, host port for the site's plain HTTP, the ACME HTTP-01 check listen empty host address for https_port and http_port: empty for every address, IPv4 and IPv6; 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 alone; 127.0.0.1 beside your own web server kcp_port 8447 with mkcp, the UDP port devices reach the relay's mKCP on kcp_header dtls with mkcp, what its packets start with, as the server's kcp_header hysteria2_port 443 with hysteria2, the UDP port devices reach the relay's Hysteria2 on

items.title: Profiles
items.text:
installation.profile=own-site: the relay serves a site of its own under its domain (--domain at init, or installation.domains), and REALITY hands it every connection without the relay's keys. It publishes port 80 too, for the certificate. The site also serves devices their subscriptions, fetched from the servers through the relay's tunnel, and XHTTP on the secret path xhttp_path, which init generates. With cdn_hosts set, relay-entry ends the relay's line with cdn=<name>,... and cdnpath=<path>, and the server gives each device a relay · cdn link through each, by a secret path of the CDNs' own (cdn_xhttp_path, generated too) that a CDN reading the requests never learns the other from (CDN in front of a relay). See Set up a relay.

installation.profile=own-site,hysteria2: the relay serves Hysteria2 on UDP hysteria2_port too, under its own site's certificate, each device's UUID its login, and carries it on to the servers like REALITY. It needs own-site, whose certificate it serves: without it the profile is refused. relay-entry then ends the relay's line with hy2=<port>, from which the server gives each device a relay · hy2 link. Open the UDP port in the provider's firewall, and replace the relay's line on the server after turning it on.

installation.profile=mkcp (with a site of its own: own-site,mkcp): the relay serves mKCP on UDP kcp_port too, under its own kcp_seed, and carries it on to the servers like REALITY. relay-entry then ends the relay's line with kcp=<port>,<header>,<seed>, from which the server gives each device a relay · kcp link. Open the UDP port in the provider's firewall, and replace the relay's line on the server after turning it on.

items.title: Secrets
items.text:
init generates the relay's own keys; the rest come from the server's relay-config.

Name Generated vless_clients no the devices the relay lets in, one <uuid> [name] per line dotdash_id no the id the relay uses on the server, its line in the server's vless_clients dotdash_encryption no the encryption= value of the server's links dotdash_short_id no the sid= value of the server's REALITY links vless_seed yes the seed the relay's VLESS Encryption key pair derives from reality_key yes the relay's REALITY private key reality_short_id yes the relay's REALITY short id kcp_seed yes the key the relay's mKCP packets are encrypted under, with mkcp

items.title: Tasks
items.text: Task relay-entry --output -- <address> the relay's line for the server's relays, and how a canary checks the relay; with no address, at entry_host facts --output the same line as JSON, which the relay publishes to an authority it follows

items.title: Server
items.text:
The dotdash bundle (ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server) runs on one Docker host outside the restricted network. Devices connect to it on 443, and it sends their traffic on through your upstream proxy, the only way out it has.

  • gate is the only container with a route out. It forwards the public ports in to Xray and carries Xray's traffic out to the upstream proxy, whose credentials only it holds.
  • Xray answers on 443 with REALITY. A dotdash device goes on through the upstream; anything else, a scanner's probe or a browser, is handed to Caddy, so 443 looks like an ordinary HTTPS site.
  • Caddy serves that site with a trusted certificate, each device's subscription URL, and XHTTP on a secret path, which is what lets XHTTP pass through a CDN.

The upstreams are the proxies and VPN exits you choose, typically ones with residential exits. With all of them down, devices get nothing, never the server's own address: what leaks where.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Install the server.
  2. Connect devices: links, an Xray config, or subscriptions.
  3. Optional:
  4. your own cover site;
  5. a DNS tunnel for networks that pass little but DNS;
  6. XHTTP with REALITY on another port;
  7. more upstreams: backups, balancing, IPv6 of its own, WireGuard and OpenVPN exits;
  8. a CDN in front of XHTTP: a local one for restricted networks, or one against address blocking;
  9. several servers sharing one set of keys.
  10. Operations: updates, alerts, backups, and moving to a new server.

items.title: CDN
items.text:
A CDN in front of this server carries XHTTP for it, and serves two different ends:

  • a local CDN, for networks that let only some addresses through: its edges are inside such a network and get through, and this server does not;
  • a CDN against address blocking: devices see only the CDN's addresses, never this server's.

items.title: A local CDN, for restricted networks
items.text:
While a network lets only some addresses through, a CDN whose edges are among them can still reach this server: devices connect to the CDN's edge, and the CDN fetches from https://example.com.

  1. At the CDN, create a resource with this server as its origin:
  2. origin https://example.com. The Host header can stay at the CDN's default: this server answers under any name. If the CDN checks the origin's certificate against a name of its own and fails, have it send example.com as the Host, or as the origin's name;
  3. no caching, and HTTP/2 towards devices if it is offered;
  4. a name devices use: the provider's own name for the resource, or a domain of yours pointed at it, with the certificate it asks for.

  5. Here, list the names devices use, comma-separated:

    sudo morzer config set cdn_hosts=cdn.example.net

  6. Devices: client-config prints a server · cdn link, the Xray config gains an outbound through it, and subscriptions pick it up. Give devices the link before restrictions start, as with a relay.

Some CDNs pass GET alone and no request body, so these links upload in small GET requests with the data in headers (XHTTP packet-up), 8 KiB at most each, under the 20 KB or so of headers a CDN takes. The server needs nothing changed for it. An app that imports the link but never connects may read its extra settings differently; the Xray config works in v2rayN and v2rayNG.

Fragile

CDNs like these break without notice, and providers act on proxy and VPN use: some refuse requests with a body, some forbid proxies in their terms, some block traffic that looks like a VPN, and an edge can stop getting through from one week to the next. Read the provider's terms, test from the networks your devices use, keep a CDN as one way among several, and expect the account to be closed.

To make losing an account cheap:

  • Spread over CDNs and accounts. cdn_hosts takes several names, and the Xray config passes over one that stops answering. Don't put every device behind one account: pools give each group of devices its own CDN hosts.
  • Serve a real site at the origin (cover site). It is what the CDN fetches and what a provider's reviewer sees. Operators report that accounts with a live, visited site behind them last longer than those fronting the bundled page.

The CDN ends one TLS connection and opens another, so it sees the requests' paths and headers. VLESS Encryption keeps what they carry from it.

A CDN is refused subscriptions. A subscription read in the clear gives away every link, the device's keys and every relay and CDN name, so one request to the provider would list every way in. The server and relays with their own site answer a subscription request a CDN passed on with the site, as any other path: its 404, or your app's answer. They recognise one by the headers a CDN adds to say so (X-Forwarded-For, Via, Forwarded and the like), which a device asking directly never sends. A CDN that adds none of them would still get one. If yours lets you add headers to its requests to the origin, add one of them, so every request it passes on says so: CDN-Loop is the one made for this, with any value, such as CDN-Loop: edge. Keep the value plain: the CDN's account shows it.

Some CDNs strip such headers, even ones you add. A relay serves subscriptions under its own domain alone, the name devices ask by, so in front of a relay have the CDN send any other name as Host: its own name, or its default. A CDN that checks the origin's certificate against that name then can't reach the relay; with a wildcard on the relay, send another name under it. Then check:

sudo morzer task run cdn-check --output

It fetches a decoy subscription, with no links in it, through each CDN in front of this server and of its relays, and prints refused for each, or SERVES SUBSCRIPTIONS for one that got it. It knows the decoy by its contents, so an app behind the site that answers every path doesn't pass for it. Keep such a CDN's name away from devices' subscriptions: an own-site relay serves them inside the restricted network with nothing in between reading them.

items.title: In front of a relay
items.text:
A CDN can front a relay with a site of its own instead of this server. The CDN's account then names the relay, which is cheap to replace, rather than this server and its upstream.

  1. At the CDN, as above, with the relay's domain as the origin: https://relay.example.net. Like the server, the relay answers under any name.

  2. On the relay, list the names devices use, then print its line again (its line); it now ends in cdn=cdn.example.net cdnpath=…:

    sudo morzer config set cdn_hosts=cdn.example.net
sudo morzer task run relay-entry --output -- <address>

  3. Here, replace the relay's line in relays (sudo morzer config edit relays). Devices get a relay · cdn link and an outbound, shaped as above, and pools take the relay's CDN names as members.

A CDN reads every request it passes on, and keeps logs. Through a relay, the links go by a path of the CDNs' own, so the CDN never learns the path devices reach the relay by directly, and they are disguised: one path, the session, sequence and padding in cookies, the padding a random token rather than a run of X, the upload under a plain header name and no event-stream type on the download, so no marker of the protocol shows by name. What it cannot hide is the shape: one visitor sending a stream of small requests beside one long download. Keep CDN links a fallback, front a relay you can replace (below), and expect a CDN account to be closed one day. A relay's line from before 0.12.0, without cdnpath=, gives the plain links by its own path. A dotdash-client with cdn=skip leaves CDN links out while it has any other.

items.title: The CDN's origin only
items.text:
Devices behind a CDN connect to the CDN's addresses, never to the relay's, so the relay behind it is not exposed the way a relay devices reach directly is. Unless you say otherwise, though, the relay's line still gives devices REALITY, XHTTP and mKCP links to its own address, which exposes it. With cdn_only=true, devices get its CDN links alone:

sudo morzer config set cdn_only=true
sudo morzer task run relay-entry --output -- <address>   # now ends in cdn-only

Replace the relay's line here again. The relay then gives devices no link or subscription URL of its own. The manager also stops judging it by its canaries, which check its own address. relay-entry refuses cdn_only without cdn_hosts, because devices would get nothing through the relay.

A network then needs one or two CDNs in all, not one per relay. Each CDN fronts one origin relay, with cdn_only=true, and the relays devices reach directly need no CDN. A CDN's origin is one host. If that relay is lost, point the CDN at another relay with a site of its own, and move cdn_hosts and cdn_only to it. The name devices use stays the same.

items.title: A CDN against address blocking
items.text: The XHTTP link works through a CDN that proxies HTTP/2 to https://example.com: put the CDN's name in the link's address. Check its terms first: many CDNs forbid proxies.

items.title: ECH
items.text:
With a CDN that offers ECH, the TLS handshake shows the CDN's public ECH name instead of example.com. Add that name to the XHTTP link, before the # (v2rayN ≥ 7.17, v2rayNG ≥ 2.0). ech.example.net stands for it here, and the DNS-over-HTTPS URL after it is where the app looks up its keys:

&ech=ech.example.net%2Bhttps%3A%2F%2F1.1.1.1%2Fdns-query

In the Xray config, add the same to that outbound's tlsSettings:

"echConfigList": "ech.example.net+https://1.1.1.1/dns-query"

With ECH set, the connection fails rather than falling back to plain SNI.

items.title: Certificates
items.text:
Every certificate a public CA issues goes into the Certificate Transparency logs, and the name in it is public from that day. Scanners read the logs for new names, look them up and probe the address. With cert_issuer=acme, each server and relay takes a certificate in its own name, so it shows up in the logs the day it starts. With the servers kept out of devices' links (direct=false), the logs are the main place a server's name still appears.

A wildcard certificate names only the parent: *.s.example.net for x7k2.s.example.net. The machine's own name stays out of the logs, and nothing there points to x7k2.

A wildcard needs a DNS-01 check, which the CA asks of your DNS. dotdash hands that check to an acme-dns server through one CNAME, so it works wherever your DNS is hosted. The credential each machine holds can answer only that one check.

items.title: Separate parents for servers and relays
items.text: Give servers and relays different parents, such as *.s.example.net and *.r.example.net or two different domains, each with its own acme-dns registration. Relays run on machines you trust less, and are replaced when burnt. A relay's credential then takes certificates under the relays' parent only, never one valid for a server's name, and a relay seen tells nothing about where the servers are.

items.title: Setting it up
items.text:
1. Names. Name each machine one label under its parent, a label nobody would guess, such as x7k2.s.example.net for a server. Point it at the machine as usual, with an A record.

  2. Registration, once per parent, on the acme-dns server:

    sudo morzer task run register --output -- s.example.net

    It prints the CNAME for step 3 and the acme_dns secret for step 4. Keep the secret as you keep the servers' keys: every machine under the parent shares it.

  3. The CNAME, once per parent, at your DNS host, as register printed it:

    _acme-challenge.s.example.net.  CNAME  <uuid>.auth.example.org.

  4. Each machine under that parent: the secret, then the issuer:

    sudo morzer secret set acme_dns       # the line register printed, then Ctrl-D
sudo morzer config set cert_issuer=acme-dns

    Caddy takes *.s.example.net over DNS-01 and serves it for the machine's name. On a relay it takes the same steps, under the own-site profile. On a new machine, give init --set cert_issuer=acme-dns and set the secret before the first apply: a single apply under acme puts the machine's name in the logs.

  5. A domain with two labels, such as example.net, has no parent to take a wildcard over. Caddy takes a certificate in its own name, over DNS-01.

  6. A name already in the logs stays there. To keep a machine out, move it to a new name under the wildcard.
  7. Port 80 stays open, for the redirect to HTTPS.
  8. If the registration is missing or malformed, Caddy doesn't start, and doctor fails the cover-site check. If the CNAME is wrong, Caddy starts but gets no certificate, and its log says why: sudo docker compose -p dotdash logs caddy.

items.title: An acme-dns server
items.text:
Run your own: whoever runs an acme-dns server can answer your domains' checks, and the public one is meant only for testing. The dotdash-acme-dns bundle is one, installed with morzer like the others.

Give it a machine of its own: the NS record that delegates its zone makes its address public, so not a dotdash server or relay, nor the manager's machine. Its zone goes under a domain apart from the servers' and the relays', such as auth.example.org: every domain it serves points a public CNAME into that zone, and one under the servers' domain would name it from the relays'.

  1. Firewall: open 53/udp, 53/tcp and 443/tcp in the provider's firewall. Install Docker and morzer as on every machine.

  2. DNS, at example.org's DNS host, before the first apply:

    acme-ns.example.org.  A   <its IP>
auth.example.org.     NS  acme-ns.example.org.

    The nameserver is outside the zone it serves, so the delegation needs no glue record, which some DNS hosts can't make.

  3. Install:

    sudo morzer init --release oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-acme-dns:stable \
  --domain auth.example.org --recovery-recipient age1… \
  --set address=<its IP> --set nameserver=acme-ns.example.org
sudo morzer apply

    address must be on the machine's own interface (ip -4 addr): ports 53 and 443 are published on it alone, apart from a local resolver on 127.0.0.53. apply waits for the API's certificate, which acme-dns takes for auth.example.org through its own DNS, so it succeeds only once the NS record above resolves.

  4. Register each parent, as in step 2 above.

Its registrations are in its data volume, which morzer's backups hold. Lose them and every parent registers again, with a new CNAME and a new secret on each machine.

items.title: Cover site
items.text:
Anyone who opens https://example.com, or probes 443, gets the cover site. The bundled page differs between servers only in its title, so one server seen reveals the others. Give each a site of its own. One parameter, cover, says what serves it:

  • pages, the default: your own files, then the bundled page;
  • an app's URL: your own files, then the app.

items.title: Your own files
items.text:
Put static files in /srv/dotdash, readable by uid 65532. Caddy serves them as they change, with no restart. For a path with no file, it serves the rest of the site: the bundled page, or the app.

sudo mkdir -p /srv/dotdash
sudo cp -r ./my-site/. /srv/dotdash/
sudo chmod -R a+rX /srv/dotdash

To keep the files elsewhere, make /srv/dotdash a symlink to that directory.

items.title: An app instead of pages
items.text:
Static pages are what a probe or a provider's reviewer expects least from a busy server. A live app, with its own routes, API answers and login wall, looks like what it is: a site in use. Name the app in cover. Caddy then passes it every request except a subscription's, XHTTP's and those for your own files.

How Caddy reaches the app depends on where it runs:

  • A container on Caddy's network, dotdash_edge, by its name. This is the one to prefer: the app needs no published port, and it never meets Xray, which is on another network.

    docker run -d --name cover-app --restart unless-stopped --network dotdash_edge <image>
sudo morzer config set cover=http://cover-app:8080

    For a container that's already running, attach it instead: docker network connect dotdash_edge <container>. In a Compose file of its own, list dotdash_edge under its networks as external: true, so the attachment survives the app being re-created.

  • Anything published on a port of the host, such as a container started with -p 8080:8080, as host.docker.internal:

    sudo morzer config set cover=http://host.docker.internal:8080

    The app must listen where containers can reach the host. That is all addresses, as -p 8080:8080 publishes, or Docker's bridge address, as -p 172.17.0.1:8080:8080 publishes. Loopback alone, 127.0.0.1, is unreachable from a container. Publishing on all addresses also opens the port to the internet, so close it in the firewall, or publish on the bridge address only.

Either way:

  • The app gets requests for this domain as Host, as behind any reverse proxy.
  • doctor checks that the app answers, asking it from inside Caddy, as Caddy does. Any HTTP answer counts, a 401 from a login wall included. With no answer, visitors get a 502, so the cover-site check fails, and config set cover=… is undone when the app it names doesn't answer.
  • cover=pages goes back to pages.

Pick something people run on servers like this one, such as a wiki, a file share or a dashboard behind a login, and give it content. The same app on every server would link them, as the bundled page does, so vary it.

items.title: An app installed with morzer
items.text:
An app shipped as a morzer bundle of its own installs beside this server as a second installation, updated and rolled back on its own. Its Compose file joins dotdash_edge as an external network, so install this server first, then the app, then point cover at it once the app reports healthy.

With two installations on the machine, morzer no longer guesses which one a command means: each names it with --product, as in sudo morzer --product dotdash config set cover=http://<app>:8080. sudo morzer shell dotdash opens a shell where every command means this server. The commands on these pages leave --product out, as they do on a machine with one installation. On a relay the product is dotdash-relay, and the network dotdash-relay_default.

items.title: DNS on devices
items.text:
The Xray config from client-config answers port-53 DNS with fake DNS: each name gets a stand-in IPv4 address from 198.18.0.0/15 at once, and a connection to it goes through the tunnel with the name, which the server looks up, as dotdash-client's TUN does. Nothing is asked of the local network, and a first visit to a name costs no round trip through the tunnel for its lookup (53 ms less in the lab at a 50 ms round trip; more behind a relay). Links leave DNS to the app.

Xray gives each answer a one-second lifetime, but some apps keep an address longer: after Xray restarts, which forgets which name each stand-in address stood for, a connection to an old one fails until the app asks for the name again.

As of November 2026:

  • v2rayNG: import as a custom config, and keep the SOCKS port at 10808.
  • v2rayN: TUN with a custom config needs the profile's "Socks port" at
  • DNS then follows v2rayN's settings, so keep them on the proxy.
  • Hiddify drops a config's DNS and routing: use the links. Its own DNS goes through the proxy by default.
  • iOS: Happ runs the config; set "Tunnel DNS" and "Include all networks". Check Streisand and V2Box on a DNS leak test site.

items.title: Devices
items.text:
Each device has its own id, a <uuid> [name] line in the vless_clients secret. init creates the first; add one per device:

uuidgen                                          # a new id
sudo EDITOR=nano morzer secret edit vless_clients  # add "<uuid> phone"; Xray restarts on save

items.title: Links and the Xray config
items.text:
sudo morzer task run client-config --output             # every device
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- phone    # one

Per device it prints:

  • an XHTTP link and a REALITY link, server · xhttp and server · reality, for each server; server · xhttp+reality with XHTTP with REALITY on; server · kcp with mKCP on; server · hy2 with Hysteria2 on; and relay · reality for each relay, with relay · xhttp before it through a relay with a site of its own, relay · cdn after that through each CDN in front of it, relay · hy2 after it through a relay with Hysteria2, and relay · kcp through a relay with mKCP; server · cdn through each CDN in front of the server. XHTTP comes first everywhere: an app tends to try the first link, and REALITY over raw TCP is the transport blocked most often. A link is named <route> · <transport>, without the device's name: its subscription is its own, and the app shows the protocol beside it. Where there are several, each is numbered, relay 1 · cdn 2: a relay by its place among the relays lines, a CDN by its place in cdn_hosts (or in its relay's cdn=), the same on every device, so an app shows no host name; with several servers, server 1, server 2 and on, in the order of servers. A relay with a name goes by it instead: edge-1 · reality;
  • an Xray config for v2rayN or v2rayNG (as a custom config) that uses whichever link answers fastest, drops a dead one within about 30 s, and falls back to the DNS tunnel when it is on, or to a standby relay's links, unchecked until then, when there is one.

The output is a password

Anyone holding a device's links can use the server as that device.

As QR codes in the terminal, with qrencode:

sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- phone | grep '^vless://' |
  while read -r link; do qrencode -t ansiutf8 "$link"; done

How each app handles DNS: DNS on devices.

items.title: Subscriptions
items.text:
With subscriptions on, each device gets one URL instead, and fetches its links from it:

sudo morzer config set subscription=true
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- phone           # its URL only
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- --full phone    # plus links and the Xray config
  • Add the URL as a subscription in the app (v2rayN, v2rayNG, Hiddify, Happ, Streisand) and refresh every few hours: revocations, key rotations and new relays then reach devices with nothing to resend.
  • An app on Apple's network stack (its User-Agent names CFNetwork, Darwin, iOS or macOS, as Shadowrocket's, Streisand's and Happ's on iOS do) gets the links with Safari's TLS hello (fp=safari), as its own platform sends; every other app, Chrome's. A Chrome hello from an iPhone fits neither its network stack nor its browser.
  • The apps that show a subscription's name (Happ, Hiddify) show the server's exit, its country's flag and IPv4 address, as the sites the device visits see it, in place of the server's domain. The server asks for it through the upstreams every ten minutes (exit_ipv4_url, exit_info_url), so after a line fails over, the next refresh shows the new exit. With upstream_mode=balance the exit changes between connections, and the name shows one of them.
  • Hiddify reads XHTTP links with its own core, which takes mode=auto as packet-up and ignores a mode in the link: long uploads through them can hang there. In Hiddify, use the REALITY or Hysteria2 link.
  • The same URL, asked with Accept: application/json, serves the device's Xray config: the client bundle runs Xray on it on a Linux machine for you. On its REALITY links, the device's UDP flows share a few connections (XUDP Mux) rather than opening one each. On every TCP link, a connection whose sent data goes unacknowledged for 15 seconds is given up and redialled: a connection the network has frozen, which XHTTP would otherwise keep sending requests down for a minute.
  • A URL is as secret as the links. sudo morzer secret rotate subscription_key moves every URL; any other path gets the site's 404.
  • A relay with a site of its own serves the same subscription inside the restricted network: client-config adds a through the relay … URL under the server's. An app takes one URL, so give a device inside the restricted network the relay's.
  • Never give a device its subscription through a CDN: the CDN would read every link.

The official sing-box apps, Karing and NekoBox can't connect to dotdash: they lack VLESS Encryption and the key share Xray's REALITY requires.

items.title: Pools
items.text:
Every device gets every relay and CDN host, so one leaked device gives away all of them. Pools split them: a device in a pool gets its pool's relays and CDN hosts, and those in no pool. One line per pool in the pools parameter: the pool's name, then its devices (their names as written in vless_clients), relay hosts (as in relays) and CDN hosts, a relay's own (its cdn= names) included:

sudo morzer config edit pools

family  mom dad relay1.example.net cdn1.example.net
friends anna boris relay2.example.net
  • A device in no pool, or without a name, gets every relay and CDN host, as before. A relay or CDN host in no pool goes to every device.
  • A relay's CDN hosts go only to devices that get the relay.
  • A device, relay or CDN host may be in several pools.
  • client-config and the subscriptions follow the change. A device that fetched its links before keeps them until it refreshes, and a device's links work through any relay, so pools hide entry points rather than lock devices out of them.
  • client-config names a member that matches no device, relay or CDN host: a typo would otherwise leave a device in no pool, and so give it everything.

Replacing a pool's relay then means new links only for that pool's devices.

items.title: Keeping the servers out of devices' links
items.text:
Pools hide relays and CDN hosts, but every device still gets the servers' own links, so one leaked device gives away every server. With direct=false devices get no server's address at all:

sudo morzer config set direct=false
  • Links and the Xray config go through relays and CDN hosts only.
  • The subscription URL is printed only through own-site relays, never on the server's domain.
  • The DNS tunnel goes: its zone is delegated to a server, so a lookup of it names the address.
  • A device that gets no relay and no CDN host gets no links, and one with no own-site relay no subscription URL. client-config names each.

Set it on every server alike: they print the same links. Relays then take the risk, and a burnt one is replaced the way a pool's is, while the servers keep their addresses. As with pools, a device that knew a server's address still reaches it: direct=false hides the servers, it does not lock devices out. To hide them from such a device too, rotate the shared keys as for revoking one.

items.title: Revoking a device
items.text:
Delete its line from vless_clients. A revoked device still knows the shared keys; to hide the server from it too, rotate them and resend links (subscriptions pick them up):

sudo morzer secret rotate reality_key
sudo morzer secret rotate vless_seed

With relays or several servers, change their copies too.

items.title: DNS tunnel
items.text:
A fallback for networks that pass little but DNS. The Xray config from client-config switches to it when the other transports fail.

ns.example.com.  A   <server IP>
t.example.com.   NS  ns.example.com.

Open 53/udp, then add --profile xdns to init, or:

sudo morzer config set installation.profile=xdns

If systemd-resolved holds port 53, set xdns_bind to the public IP.

items.title: A domain of its own
items.text:
Better: a resolver that flags tunnel queries blocks the domain above them, which would take the site with it. Use a cheap, unrelated domain (example.net) for nothing but the tunnel:

; at example.net's DNS provider
ns.example.net.  A   <server IP>
t.example.net.   NS  ns.example.net.

dig +short NS t.example.net                       # ns.example.net. once delegated
sudo morzer config set xdns_domain=t.example.net
sudo morzer task run client-config --output -- --full phone   # resend: the config names the zone

items.title: Hysteria2
items.text:
A link over QUIC on a UDP port of its own (hysteria2_port, 443), for a network that lets UDP through. Hysteria2 runs in the server's own Xray, so it needs no other software. To the network it looks like an HTTP/3 connection to your domain, under the site's own certificate: a client that brings no login gets the cover site over HTTP/3. Open the UDP port in the provider's firewall, then:

sudo morzer config set installation.profile=hysteria2   # with the DNS tunnel: xdns,hysteria2

Each device gets a server · hy2 link and an outbound in the Xray config. Its login is the device's own UUID, so revoking a device in vless_clients revokes it here too.

  • Clients: Happ, v2rayN, v2rayNG, Hiddify, Streisand, mihomo and the sing-box apps read hysteria2:// links. dotdash-client takes it from its subscription like any other outbound.
  • One address, two families. Some networks block a server's whole address for minutes after they see UDP to it from abroad. That would take its TCP links with it, so give Hysteria2 a server, or an address, of its own where you can, and measure it on a canary (--profile hysteria2) before relying on it.
  • hysteria2_up: 0 by default: Hysteria2 runs BBR, which backs off on loss as TCP does. Set it to the Mbit/s each device may get, and a device that asks for a rate gets Brutal: a steady send at that rate whatever is lost, which holds up on lossy mobile links. Never set it above what the server's uplink can give each device, or it floods the line.
  • A frozen connection. When a network stops passing a connection without closing it, a device gives it up after 15 s of silence and opens a new one. The Xray config devices get sends a keepalive every few seconds, so a connection idle that long stays open; a client from the hysteria2:// link keeps its own keepalives, and without any closes an idle connection after 15 s, with whatever it carried, then reconnects.
  • The certificate is Caddy's: Xray reads it from Caddy's data and reloads it hourly. Under this profile Caddy starts first, and on a fresh install Xray retries until Caddy has taken the certificate, which takes seconds with Let's Encrypt.

Off: set the previous profile (xdns) or sudo morzer config unset installation.profile, before any rollback to a release without it.

A relay with a site of its own serves Hysteria2 too (installation.profile=own-site,hysteria2 on the relay, see its reference): devices then get a relay · hy2 link through it, whether or not this server runs the profile.

items.title: Install
items.text:
You need a domain, a Linux host outside the restricted network, and an upstream proxy. example.com stands for your domain throughout.

  1. DNS: point the domain at the server:

    example.com.  A  <server IP>

    Every certificate the server takes names its domain in public logs. A name one label under a parent kept for servers, such as x7k2.s.example.com, can later take a wildcard that keeps it out of them, and keeps the servers apart from relays: see Certificates.

  2. Firewall: open 80/tcp and 443/tcp in the cloud provider's firewall (a VPC firewall rule, on some clouds). Docker's published ports bypass ufw and firewalld, so the provider's firewall is the one that counts. Allow SSH with keys only.

  3. Host: install Docker, sops, age and morzer, with bootstrap.sh on Debian or Ubuntu.

  4. Recovery key: it decrypts the backups. Make it, and keep it off the machine:

    morzer secret recipients generate-recovery-key ~/dotdash-recovery.key

    It prints the public half, age1…, which the next step takes.

  5. Deploy:

    sudo morzer init --release oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server:stable \
  --domain example.com --recovery-recipient age1…
sudo morzer secret set upstreams    # socks5://user:pass@host:port, one per line
sudo morzer apply
    • upstreams lists the ways out, one per line, in order: socks5://, socks5+tls://, http:// or https:// and user:pass@host:port, or a WireGuard or OpenVPN exit's wireguard:// or openvpn:// line. The first that answers carries the traffic. See Upstreams for backups, IPv6, WireGuard and OpenVPN.
    • Changing proxy later is one secret edit upstreams and one restart.
    • init prints the release's signing key and trusts it. To check even this first release against the key published with the repository, add --signing-key "$(gh variable get MINISIGN_RELEASE_PUBKEY -R morzecrew/dotdash)".

  6. Check: apply succeeds only once Xray reaches the internet through the upstream and 443 serves the site with a trusted certificate. Later, at any time:

    sudo morzer doctor                        # health, and the failing layer if any
sudo morzer task run exit-check --output  # the exit sites see

Next: connect devices.

items.title: What leaks where
items.text:
• Traffic leaves only through the upstream. With the upstream down, clients get nothing, never this server's address, unless upstreams holds a direct line, which makes this server's address an exit on purpose. Xray has no route out; a gate container holds the upstream's credentials. Every apply, update and doctor checks this against what runs.
  • The upstream sees destination addresses, ports and volume, not hostnames: this server resolves them over DoH (dns_resolver), through the upstream. SNI stays visible unless the client uses ECH. resolve=upstream hands the upstream the hostnames.
  • On the device, only the app keeps traffic inside a dropped tunnel (TUN with a kill switch, or Android's "block connections without VPN"). A browser IP checker showing an IPv6 address that exit-check calls unavailable sees the device's own: route IPv6 into the tunnel or turn it off in the app.
  • To keep IPv6 out altogether, set ipv6=block where it applies: on a client it is refused on the machine, on a relay it ends there, and here no IPv6 destination leaves (parameters).

items.title: WebRTC
items.text:
A browser's WebRTC asks a STUN server, over UDP, which address it sees, and a page can read the answer (the server-reflexive candidate). What it gets depends on how the device reaches dotdash (dotdash-lab #52 measured each):

The device The server carries UDP (upstream_udp) WebRTC's address A browser set to a proxy port (dotdash-client's, or an app's) either the device's own: STUN leaves around the proxy The same, with the WebRtcIPHandling policy below either none, and no candidate at all Behind a TUN (dotdash-client's tun, an app in VPN mode) yes the exit's, as the rest of its traffic Behind a TUN no (the default) none: only a local candidate

  • On a proxy port, set Chromium's WebRtcIPHandling policy to disable_non_proxied_udp, or better, use the TUN. The policy stops the leak but leaves a browser with no WebRTC address at all, which a page can notice. Chromium's old --force-webrtc-ip-handling-policy switch is gone: the policy goes in a managed policy file (on Linux, /etc/chromium/policies/managed/ or /etc/opt/chrome/policies/managed/):

    {"WebRtcIPHandling": "disable_non_proxied_udp"}

  • Behind a TUN, nothing leaks. With upstream_udp=true (every upstream line then has to carry UDP), WebRTC's address is the exit's. Without it, WebRTC has no public address, a smaller tell than a leaked one.

  • A canary reports per transport whether the server carries UDP (udp in its facts).
  • DNS stays inside in both modes: browsers send names to a SOCKS proxy, and client-config's Xray config and dotdash-client's TUN answer port 53 themselves.

items.title: The browser's location
items.text:
dotdash keeps the network consistent: sites see the exit IP, and geolocation by IP follows it. The browser can still tell another story. JavaScript's timezone (Date, Intl) and the Geolocation API read the device's own settings, not the exit. To match them to the exit without changing the device's settings, use a browser extension that sets both:

  • Cloaq, for desktop Chromium. It sets them through Chrome's debugger API (Emulation.setTimezoneOverride and setGeolocationOverride), in the engine, so a page finds no JavaScript wrapper to detect: Chrome Web Store.
  • GeoSpoof, to match the exit's region in one click (VPN Sync), or on mobile:
    • Chrome Web Store, for desktop Chromium;
    • Firefox Add-ons, for desktop Firefox and Firefox for Android 140 and later;
    • App Store, for Safari on iOS, iPadOS and macOS.

Neither needs the proxy's credentials: they read the exit IP, or take a region. Both are optional. Neither stops WebRTC from showing the device's own addresses, which is a browser setting of its own.

Chrome on Android takes no extensions, so use Firefox for Android there. GeoSpoof's Google Play app is a different thing: it fakes the device's GPS for every app, as its "Mock location app" in Developer options, rather than working in the browser.

items.title: mKCP
items.text:
A link over UDP on its own port (kcp_port, 8447), for a network that blocks the TCP transports but lets UDP through. mKCP has no TLS underneath: its packets are encrypted under the kcp_seed secret and start with a fake header (kcp_header), so they look like neither KCP nor TLS. VLESS Encryption still protects what they carry. Open the UDP port in the provider's firewall, then:

sudo morzer config set installation.profile=mkcp   # with the DNS tunnel: xdns,mkcp

Each device gets a server · kcp link and an outbound in the Xray config.

  • Clients: v2rayN and v2rayNG. mihomo has no mKCP: it treats the link as TCP, which never answers, and its health check skips it. sing-box apps can't use it either.
  • kcp_header: dtls by default: each packet starts as a DTLS 1.2 record, as WebRTC calls and some VPNs send. wireguard starts it as WireGuard data; utp and wechat as those; srtp is Xray's own, which doesn't start as real RTP does; none sends bare encrypted packets. No header is known to pass everywhere: if one is blocked, try another, then let devices refresh their subscription or send them new links.
  • Bandwidth: mKCP resends lost packets eagerly, so on a lossy line it uses more than TCP would. The Xray config picks it, as any other link, whenever it answers fastest.

Off: set the previous profile (xdns) or sudo morzer config unset installation.profile, before any rollback to a release without it.

items.title: Moving to a new server
items.text:
Prepare: keep the recovery key off the machine, add a backup target, and set the A record's TTL to 300 s or less. Devices keep their links.

# on the new server, after bootstrap.sh
sudo morzer --product dotdash installation import --from-backup \
  --target s3://bucket/dotdash --credentials-file ./bucket.yaml \
  --identity ~/dotdash-recovery.key
sudo morzer update oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server:stable
# optional, keeps Caddy's certificate (import prints both ids)
sudo morzer backup fetch <backup id>
sudo morzer restore --force --confirm <installation id> --identity ~/dotdash-recovery.key

Then point example.com (and ns.example.com) at the new IP and shut the old machine down: two live servers with one installation id confuse each other's backups.

items.title: Operations
items.text:
Updates, alerts, backups and doctor work the same on relay, client and canary machines; only the update channel names another bundle.

Task Command Update by hand sudo morzer update --stage && sudo morzer update --to <version> New morzer sudo morzer self-update Backups off the machine sudo morzer backup target add s3://bucket/dotdash --credentials backup_s3 Alerts sudo morzer notify target add https://hooks.example/morzer Health and faults sudo morzer doctor Which exit sites see sudo morzer task run exit-check --output Whether each CDN is refused subscriptions sudo morzer task run cdn-check --output Metrics for Prometheus sudo morzer config set metrics.textfile=/var/lib/prometheus/node-exporter

items.title: Unattended updates
items.text:
From :stable, nightly at 03:30.

Warning

This gives whoever holds the release key root on the machine.

sudo morzer config set update.check=true
sudo morzer config set update.channel=oci://ghcr.io/morzecrew/dotdash-server:stable
sudo morzer config set update.auto_apply=true

items.title: Managed from elsewhere
items.text:
A machine can follow an authority, an operator key that publishes what it should hold, as morzer describes it. Each bundle names what an authority may set; everything else stays the machine's own.

Bundle An authority may set It tells the authority (facts) server vless_clients, the shared keys (reality_key, vless_seed, reality_short_id, xhttp_path, kcp_seed, subscription_key), servers, relays, cdn_hosts, pools, subscription, direct its domain and ports, the REALITY public key and the VLESS encryption string relay vless_clients, dotdash_id, dotdash_encryption, dotdash_short_id, dotdash_servers, dotdash_address, dotdash_port, dotdash_public_key, ipv6 its relay-entry line, at entry_host canary every dotdash_* nothing client subscription_url, proxy_password nothing

The upstreams stay each server's own. A relay's facts carry the short id, and with own-site or mkcp the XHTTP path or the mKCP seed: the credentials its devices' links carry anyway. sudo morzer task run facts --output prints them.

items.title: Pin the exit IP
items.text:
doctor fails when the provider moves you:

sudo morzer config set probe_url=https://api.ipify.org 'probe_expect=^203\.0\.113\.7\s*$'

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
With morzer's own metrics in the node exporter's textfile directory (metrics.textfile), the metrics profile adds Xray's and the gate's's, in the same directory: each one's traffic per inbound and outbound, and the gate's verdicts on its upstreams. Nothing is counted per device. The exporters run as 65532, so the directory has to be writable by it:

sudo setfacl -m u:65532:rwx /var/lib/prometheus/node-exporter
sudo morzer config set metrics_textfile=/var/lib/prometheus/node-exporter   # its default
sudo morzer config set installation.profile=xdns,metrics    # beside the profiles you run
Metric Labels Value dotdash_xray_up role 1 when the exporter read Xray's counters dotdash_inbound_bytes_total role, inbound, direction bytes through an inbound since Xray started dotdash_outbound_bytes_total role, outbound, direction bytes through an outbound since Xray started dotdash_observatory_alive role, outbound 1 when the last check got through an upstream dotdash_observatory_delay_seconds role, outbound that check's time, while it gets through dotdash_xray_heap_bytes role Xray's Go heap, beside its GOMEMLIMIT

Every series also carries product. rate(dotdash_inbound_bytes_total[5m]) per inbound shows which transport devices use, and one falling to zero while the others carry on is what a block on it looks like.

items.title: What the checks say
items.text:
• Alerts cover failed applies, updates and backups, and each morning's doctor, which names the failing layer: the proxy's address, its credentials, the destination, or the exit.
  • exit-check: "IPv6 unavailable" means the upstream has no IPv6 exit, which is not a leak. "MISMATCH" means IPv4 and IPv6 leave from different networks.
  • Backups run nightly: secrets, encrypted to the recovery key, and Caddy's certificates. See morzer's operating docs.
