items.title: Secrets
items.text:
init generates every secret except the ways out, upstreams. Set it with sudo morzer secret set <name>, edit with sudo morzer secret edit <name>, replace a generated one with sudo morzer secret rotate <name>.

Name Generated upstreams no every way out, one per line, in order (Upstreams); required vless_clients yes one <uuid> [name] line per device vless_seed yes ML-KEM-768 seed the VLESS Encryption key pair derives from acme_dns no with cert_issuer=acme-dns, the acme-dns registration as JSON (Certificates) reality_key yes REALITY private key (x25519) reality_short_id yes REALITY short id clients present alongside the key xhttp_path yes secret path Caddy routes to Xray's XHTTP inbound subscription_key yes key the subscription URLs derive from kcp_seed yes key mKCP's packets are encrypted under reality_key_second no with reality_second_key, a second REALITY private key (Rotating the REALITY key) reality_short_id_second no with reality_second_key, the short id that goes with it

Rotating vless_seed, reality_key, reality_short_id or xhttp_path changes every link, and kcp_seed the mKCP links: resend them, or let subscriptions pick it up.

items.title: Rotating the REALITY key
items.text:
secret rotate reality_key cuts off every device until it has the new links. With reality_second_key, the server accepts a second key beside reality_key, so devices holding either get in, and the key can change with no one cut off. A prober meets the site through both, as before.

  1. The next key, second. Make a key pair and a short id, and set them as the second key. Devices keep working, and links still carry the current key. Put a canary on the next key (dotdash_public_key and dotdash_short_id) and check that it gets through:

    sudo docker run --rm ghcr.io/morzecrew/xray:26.11.9 x25519    # PrivateKey, and Password, its public half
openssl rand -hex 8 | sudo morzer secret set reality_short_id_second
sudo morzer secret set reality_key_second                      # paste the PrivateKey
sudo morzer config set reality_second_key=true

  2. Swap. Set the next key and short id as reality_key and reality_short_id, and the old ones as the second key. Links and subscriptions now carry the new key, and devices still on the old one keep getting in.

  3. Retire the old key. Once subscriptions have refreshed and you've resent links (devices fetch a subscription every hour by default), turn the second key off:

    sudo morzer config set reality_second_key=false

With relays or several servers, set the same keys on each server, and move relays to the new key (dotdash_public_key, dotdash_short_id) between steps 2 and 3.

items.title: Several servers
items.text:
Same keys on every server, each under its own domain and the same https_port. Links then cover every server, and the Xray config fails over between them. Add and revoke devices on each.

# on the first server; sudo on b.example.com must not prompt
for s in vless_clients vless_seed reality_key reality_short_id xhttp_path; do
  sudo cat /run/dotdash/secrets/$s | ssh b.example.com sudo morzer secret set $s
done
# on every server
sudo morzer config set servers=example.com,b.example.com

items.title: Beside your own web server
items.text:
A machine whose own Caddy already holds 80 and 443 for other sites can run a dotdash server or relay too. The web server keeps both ports. It reads the server name in each TLS ClientHello and passes the connections for dotdash's names through to it untouched, as REALITY needs. Every other connection goes on to its sites as before.

dotdash then publishes on loopback, on spare ports:

sudo morzer config set listen=127.0.0.1 https_port=9443 http_port=9080 entry_port=443

entry_port=443 keeps devices', relays' and the canary's links on 443, the port they reach the web server on. A relay needs no entry_port: devices always dial a relay on 443. Set listen and https_port, and http_port under own-site.

items.title: The web server
items.text:
Caddy needs the layer4 module, which upstream's builds leave out. The caddy-l4 image of platform-images has it: run that image on the host network in place of the package, or copy its binary out, as its README shows.

{
    servers :443 {
        listener_wrappers {
            layer4 {
                @dotdash tls sni s.example.net r1.example.net
                route @dotdash {
                    proxy 127.0.0.1:9443
                }
            }
            tls
        }
    }
}

# Only under cert_issuer=acme: its HTTP-01 check. acme-dns needs neither.
http://s.example.net {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:9080
}

A server and a relay on one machine each get their own @matcher and route, to their own https_port. Under cert_issuer=acme-dns dotdash takes its certificate over DNS and needs nothing from the web server's port 80.

items.title: What changes
items.text:
• The web server's restarts drop dotdash's connections too.
  • dotdash sees every connection come from the web server, never the device's address. It keeps none either way.
  • A CDN in front of the server must send its domain as the server name. Under a name of the CDN's own, the connection goes to the web server's sites instead.
  • A relay's site must not be one of the web server's own names: the relay sends probes to its site, and the web server would hand them straight back to the relay.
  • The mKCP, DNS tunnel and XHTTP with REALITY ports are the machine's own and don't pass through the web server.
  • listen is one address, or empty, the default, for every address, IPv4 and IPv6. 0.0.0.0 publishes on every IPv4 address and no IPv6 one.
  • Before an apply starts dotdash, morzer checks every port it is about to publish on that port's own address and protocol, a profile's ports too (UDP for the DNS tunnel, mKCP and Hysteria2), and refuses to start with one taken, naming what holds it.

items.title: Upstreams
items.text:
Every connection leaves through the ways out the upstreams secret lists: proxies, WireGuard exits and OpenVPN exits, one per line, in order. A change of provider, a backup or a second exit is one edit of that secret.

sudo morzer secret edit upstreams

# [name=<name>] [group=<group>] [warm=<n>] | <url>
name=isp-a | socks5://alice:secret@203.0.113.7:1080
name=isp-b | https://bob:secret@proxy.example.net:443
name=home  | wireguard://<private key>@198.51.100.4:51820?publickey=<base64>&address=10.34.0.3/32
name=vpn   | openvpn://H4sIAAAAAAACA…
socks5://carol:secret@203.0.113.8:1080
A line Way out socks5://[user:pass@]host:port a SOCKS5 proxy socks5+tls://[user:pass@]host:port a SOCKS5 proxy over TLS http://[user:pass@]host:port an HTTP proxy https://[user:pass@]host:port an HTTP proxy over TLS wireguard://… a WireGuard exit, from its wg-quick file (below) openvpn://… an OpenVPN exit, from its client config (below) direct this server's own address (below)
  • After the scheme, a proxy is user:pass@host:port, or host:port with no login. The password may contain : and @, and is not percent-encoded. An IPv6 host goes in brackets.
  • Tags go before the URL, ending in |; a line with none is its URL alone. Lines written with the tags after the URL, as before, still work.
  • name= is optional, lowercase letters, digits and dashes. doctor and the gate's log name each line by it, and upstream_pin takes it.
  • warm=<n> keeps a proxy's connections ready ahead of use (below).
  • Blank lines and # lines are skipped.

Proxies with residential exits suit this best. With every line down, devices get nothing, never the server's own address: what leaks where.

items.title: No upstream: this server's own address
items.text:
A server that is itself on the network traffic should leave from, such as a home line with a residential address, needs no proxy in between: the line direct makes its own address a way out.

name=home | direct
  • Alone, every connection leaves from this server's address, and devices see it as their exit.
  • Beside proxies, it is a line like any other, probed with them and ordered by upstream_mode and upstream_pin: first with a proxy as its backup, or last as a fallback. A fallback means that, with every proxy down, traffic leaves from this server's address instead of not at all, which What leaks where otherwise rules out.
  • It takes name= and group=ipv6 (the server's own IPv6, under ipv6=separate), not warm=. It carries UDP, so upstream_udp works with it.
  • resolve=gateway keeps resolving names over dns_resolver, now from this address; resolve=upstream leaves them to this machine's resolver.
  • When nothing gets out, doctor fetches probe_url from this machine directly for that line.

items.title: Order and modes
items.text:
The gate probes every line through it, fetching probe_url, every 10 seconds, so every line sees that URL's host name; with resolve=gateway, clients' destinations still reach them as addresses. A line whose answer takes more than 1.5 seconds counts as down, as one that doesn't answer: a line throttled that hard would add a second or more to every connection. One failed probe is enough, so a line that goes silent takes new connections for about 8 seconds on average, 12 at most, before they move to another. When no line answers, connections still take the first one rather than none, so a wrong verdict, or a single line that is only slow, never stops the traffic; a line that is really down fails them itself. upstream_mode decides how the lines that answer share the traffic:

upstream_mode failover (default) the first line while it answers, so the exit stays put; when it doesn't, the fastest of the rest, and back to the first once it answers again fastest whichever line answers fastest balance every line that answers, each connection to any of them
  • A failed line moves connections within about a minute. Connections open at that moment break, and apps reconnect.
  • The exit changes with the line. Lines in one country keep geolocated sites behaving the same. Under balance, one site may see several exits in a session, which some sites answer with a captcha or a new login.
  • sudo morzer config set upstream_pin=isp-b puts that line first whatever its place, the others behind it as the mode has them; none (the default) keeps the file's order.
  • doctor passes while any line carries. exit-check shows the exit in use. If you pin the exit IP, match every line's address to stay quiet when another carries, such as 'probe_expect=^(203\.0\.113\.7|198\.51\.100\.9)\s*$'.

items.title: IPv6
items.text:
ipv6 decides where IPv6 destinations go:

ipv6 allow (default) through the lines like any other: right when every line has IPv6 separate through the lines marked group=ipv6, with upstream_mode applying to them alone, and never through the others block nowhere: names resolve to IPv4 only, so dual-stack sites still work over IPv4

A proxy carries IPv6 when its own host has it. A WireGuard exit does when its address holds an IPv6 address and its exit routes IPv6, and an OpenVPN exit when its server pushes IPv6. For IPv4-only proxies and a provider's separate IPv6 one:

name=isp-a              | socks5://alice:secret@203.0.113.7:1080
name=isp-a6 group=ipv6  | socks5://alice:secret@[2001:db8::7]:1080

sudo morzer config set ipv6=separate
sudo morzer task run exit-check --output

Destinations with an IPv6 address, dual-stack ones included, leave through the IPv6 lines, the rest through the others, and neither falls back to the other. A dual-stack WireGuard exit can serve both: group=upstream,ipv6. separate needs resolve=gateway (the default); two providers show as MISMATCH in exit-check, as expected.

items.title: WireGuard
items.text:
The wireguard-line task turns a wg-quick file, as a router or a provider exports it, into its line:

sudo morzer task run wireguard-line --output --input conf=./wg0.conf

wireguard://oIpc…%3D@vpn.example:51820?publickey=n9B5…%3D&address=10.34.0.3%2F32&allowedips=0.0.0.0%2F0%2C::%2F0&keepalive=25
  • Add it to upstreams, with a name= if you like. The line holds the private key: treat it as the file.
  • One [Peer] per line: a file with several needs splitting first.
  • The gate runs Xray's own WireGuard, on its built-in network stack, so it needs no extra privilege. DNS, PostUp and the like are left out: this server resolves names itself and runs no scripts.
  • A link an app shares works too: wireguard://<key>@host:port?publickey=…&address=…, with mtu, presharedkey, keepalive and allowedips (all of 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0 unless given).

items.title: OpenVPN
items.text:
Up to 8 OpenVPN exits, one per line. They run in a container of their own, which the openvpn profile adds, each tunnel on its own device. A line holds the exit's client config, with its keys inline (<ca>, <cert>, <key>, <tls-crypt>), and a provider's login goes inline too:

<auth-user-pass>
user
password
</auth-user-pass>

The openvpn-line task turns the config into its line:

sudo morzer task run openvpn-line --output --input conf=./client.ovpn

openvpn://H4sIAAAAAAACA0vOyUzNK-HlSkktUygpzePl…

Before an update from a release without the task, make it by hand:

printf 'openvpn://%s\n' "$(gzip -c client.ovpn | base64 -w0 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')"

Add the line, then turn the profile on. Until then the line leads nowhere and the other lines carry the traffic:

sudo morzer secret edit upstreams                       # add the line, with "name=vpn | " before it if you like
sudo morzer config set installation.profile=openvpn    # with others, all of them: xdns,openvpn
sudo morzer task run exit-check --output
  • The line holds the keys: treat it as the config.
  • Before OpenVPN starts, its container's default route is replaced by routes to the servers in the configs, so nothing leaves around a tunnel, even while it connects. No tunnel takes a default route: each line's traffic leaves through its own tunnel alone, and goes nowhere while that tunnel is down. Every apply and doctor checks that the container has no default route around the tunnels.
  • It runs as root with NET_ADMIN and /dev/net/tun, the one container here that does: OpenVPN takes nothing less. It reads its lines from the upstreams secret, which is the gate's, with DAC_READ_SEARCH.
  • An edit of upstreams restarts it, and every tunnel with it. If an OpenVPN exits, it starts again within a minute, and nothing leaves through it while it is down; the other tunnels carry on.
  • A config can't run scripts, or send OpenVPN's log anywhere but docker logs. The servers' addresses are looked up when the container starts: a provider that moves its server is reached again after sudo morzer restart vpn.
  • The server's kernel must be Linux 5.7 or newer, which lets the SOCKS hop beside the tunnels send each line's traffic into its own tunnel without privilege.
  • To drop them, turn the profile off, then remove the lines. The other way round, the container restarts with no line to run, and refuses.

Exits must be outside the restricted network

WireGuard and OpenVPN are easy to detect and block. Between this server and an exit outside that doesn't matter; an exit inside the restricted network would be blocked, and would send the traffic back where it came from.

items.title: Warm connections
items.text:
Every new connection pays a proxy's handshake before a site's first byte leaves: four round trips to a SOCKS5 proxy that takes a login (TCP, greeting, login, CONNECT), two to an HTTP proxy. With the proxy 35 ms from the server, that adds 140 ms, or 70 ms, to every connection of every page.

Tagged warm=<n>, a proxy line goes through the warm profile's container, which keeps n connections to the proxy open and logged in. A new connection's CONNECT leaves with its first bytes on one of them, so the handshake costs it nothing. Measured from a server 34 ms from its proxy, the first byte of a fetch came after 203 ms without, and after 51 ms with a connection ready.

name=isp-a warm=4 | socks5://alice:secret@203.0.113.7:1080

Turn the profile on, then tag the line. A tagged line leads nowhere until the container runs:

sudo morzer config set installation.profile=warm    # with others, all of them: xdns,warm
sudo morzer secret edit upstreams                   # add warm=4 to the line's tags
  • n is 1 to 16. Each new connection takes one ready connection, and another opens in its place. A burst past n sends its greeting, login and CONNECT in one go, one round trip instead of four. A provider that limits how many connections you hold at once counts the ready ones too.
  • A ready connection is replaced after 90 seconds, or as soon as the proxy closes it. If one turns out dead when used, the connection goes again on a new one.
  • The proxy must take a connection's first bytes sent right after its CONNECT, before it replies. Most do; through one that doesn't, every connection fails. Remove the tag, and the line's connections go straight from the gate again.
  • With upstream_udp=true, a SOCKS5 line's UDP goes through the container too, with UDP associations kept ready once a device first sends UDP.
  • The container holds the tagged lines' logins, as the gate does, and an edit of upstreams restarts it. It is on the gate's network alone, never beside Xray, which every apply and doctor checks.
  • WireGuard and OpenVPN lines take no warm=: they have no handshake per connection.
  • To drop it, remove the tags, then turn the profile off.

items.title: UDP
items.text:
upstream_udp=true carries devices' UDP, such as calls and QUIC, through the lines. Every line must carry it then: a WireGuard or OpenVPN line, or a SOCKS5 proxy with UDP ASSOCIATE; an HTTP proxy drops it. Off, UDP is dropped here and apps fall back to TCP.

Every apply, update and doctor refuses upstream_udp=true with an HTTP or HTTPS proxy line. Whether a SOCKS5 proxy relays UDP shows only by trying it: a canary reports udp per transport in its facts.

items.title: What doctor says
items.text: When nothing gets out, doctor asks the first lines directly and names each by its name=: one that doesn't answer, one that refused the credentials in its line, a WireGuard peer that didn't carry it, an OpenVPN tunnel that is down, a warm= line whose container isn't running. A line that answers when asked directly points at the gate instead.

items.title: XHTTP with REALITY
items.text:
A third link on its own port (xhttp_reality_port, 8443), for a network that passes another port better than 443. Xray-core clients (v2rayN, v2rayNG) and mihomo. Open the port in the provider's firewall, then:

sudo morzer config set installation.profile=xhttp-reality   # with the DNS tunnel: xdns,xhttp-reality

Off: set the previous profile (xdns) or sudo morzer config unset installation.profile, before any rollback to a release without it.
